title: Hospice and Palliative Medicine Fellowship Program
prerequisites: Intended for physicians in postgraduate medical education or clinicians with foundational pathophysiology, pharmacology, ethics, and communication training.
Ability to read professional clinical guidance critically and distinguish evidence, policy, and institution-specific operations.
For any real clinical application: appropriate license, local supervision, institutional policies, and specialty consultation are required; this course supplies none.
No prerequisite or completion of this course creates board eligibility.
objectives: Apply the published HPM blueprint as a study map while acknowledging its limits.
Perform a structured whole-person assessment of serious illness in fictional educational scenarios.
Explain symptom-management reasoning, risk reassessment, and indications for escalation without issuing patient-specific orders.
Communicate prognosis uncertainty, respond to emotion, elicit values, and build a goal-concordant plan in simulated cases.
Differentiate palliative care, hospice care, and the U.S. Medicare hospice benefit.
Recognize emergency/refractory symptom categories and the limits of independent learning.
Plan interdisciplinary transitions across settings and recognize caregiver, equity, and cultural needs.
Critically appraise evidence and propose a small quality-improvement question.

units.title: Serious illness, trajectories, and prognostication
objectives: Compare trajectories and uncertainty across cancer and noncancer serious illness.
Frame prognostic reasoning as an estimate and communicate what is known, unknown, and functionally relevant.
Relate potential disease-directed interventions to benefits and burdens.
boardDomains: Prognostication and Natural History of Serious and Complex Illness (10%)
units.casePractice: Fictional, de-identified-on-purpose vignette: formulate a conditional prognosis and list information needed before a recommendation; do not make a real-patient prediction.
units.assessment: Short written uncertainty statement and evidence/assumption audit.

units.title: Comprehensive whole-person assessment
objectives: Elicit pain and non-pain symptoms, function, capacity/development, culture, supports, and stressors.
Distinguish symptom report from sign and document uncertainty.
Integrate physical, psychosocial, spiritual, financial, and caregiver needs into one problem list.
units.casePractice: Linked authentic home-transition report is used only by URL; identify assessment domains missing from the published summary.
units.assessment: Structured whole-person assessment template scored with a checklist.

units.title: Managing pain and non-pain symptoms
objectives: Classify pain and identify symptoms requiring reassessment or specialist input.
Explain multimodal symptom-management reasoning while recognizing organ dysfunction, adverse effects, and substance-use risk.
Avoid mechanically applying non-palliative opioid guidance to cancer, palliative, or end-of-life care.
units.casePractice: Use the NCI professional summary to compare symptom patterns, red flags, and data gaps; no prescribing exercise or dose calculation.
units.assessment: Mechanism-and-risk concept map plus two original MCQs.

units.title: Psychological, social, spiritual, cultural, and family care
objectives: Recognize psychological, existential, social, cultural, and caregiver distress as clinical concerns.
Use an interdisciplinary referral plan rather than treating spiritual or social needs as an afterthought.
Practice language that elicits values without stereotyping culture or family structure.
boardDomains: Comprehensive Whole-Patient Assessment; Managing Suffering and Distress; Interdisciplinary Teamwork, Quality, and Professionalism
units.casePractice: Discuss the licensed pediatric serious-illness case by link; create a role map (family, social work, chaplaincy, nursing, primary team) without copying its text or images.
units.assessment: Reflective note that separates observed facts, patient values, clinician assumptions, and referral needs.

units.title: Communication, advance care planning, capacity, and ethics
objectives: Respond to emotion, communicate uncertainty, elicit goals, and summarize a shared plan.
Differentiate decision-making capacity assessment from agreement with a clinician.
Identify why legal and ethical rules, including medical aid-in-dying law, are jurisdiction-specific.
boardDomains: Communication Skills (2%); Ethical and Legal Aspects of Care (7%)
units.casePractice: Use a fictional scenario to script a values question, an uncertainty statement, and a next-step summary; no legal advice.
units.assessment: Recorded or written simulated-family-meeting opening, assessed for empathy, clarity, uncertainty, and follow-up.

units.title: Medical interventions and goal-concordant transitions
objectives: Describe a structured approach to discussing continuation, withholding, or withdrawal of interventions.
Anticipate symptom, psychosocial, spiritual, and team needs before a transition.
Distinguish hospice-benefit decisions from palliative consultation.
boardDomains: Management of Medical Interventions (6%); Ethical and Legal Aspects of Care (7%)
units.casePractice: Fictional care-conference: map who needs to be present, facts to clarify, and documentation elements before a transition.
units.assessment: Goal-concordance decision map; no procedural authorization or medication order.

units.title: Palliative emergencies and refractory symptoms
objectives: Recognize emergency categories and describe triage, anticipatory planning, and communication priorities.
Differentiate potentially reversible causes from refractory distress in an educational framework.
State why proportional palliative sedation is a specialist, context-dependent response for refractory symptoms—not a routine shortcut.
boardDomains: Palliative Care Emergencies and Refractory Symptoms (5%)
units.casePractice: Time-limited fictional triage table: immediate safety/escalation, information needed, family communication, and team roles.
units.assessment: Open-book emergency recognition quiz; answers must cite an authoritative source.

units.title: Imminent dying, death event, grief, and bereavement
objectives: Recognize that symptom trajectory, communication capacity, and family needs change near death.
Prepare families using clear, non-deterministic language and attend to cultural/spiritual preferences.
Identify when grief/bereavement support or referral is needed.
boardDomains: Impending Death and the Death Event (3%); Grief, Loss, and Bereavement (3%)
units.casePractice: NCI Last Days reading annotation: label statements that require individualized assessment; do not turn them into a prediction tool.
units.assessment: Family-preparation communication checklist and brief bereavement referral rationale.

units.title: Hospice regulation, care settings, and safe transitions
objectives: Explain the specific U.S. Medicare hospice-benefit criteria without equating them with all palliative care.
Compare inpatient, ambulatory, home, long-term-care, and hospice settings.
Design a safe handoff that addresses medications, caregiver capacity, equipment, and 24-hour support.
boardDomains: Quality and Compliance (2%); Interdisciplinary Teamwork, Quality, and Professionalism (2%)
units.casePractice: Analyze the anonymized published home-discharge case at the original URL and list transition risks; links only, no rehosting.
units.assessment: Hospice-versus-palliative comparison and handoff checklist.

units.title: Interdisciplinary teamwork, quality, scholarship, and pediatric scope
objectives: Define functions of interdisciplinary team members and lead a respectful case review.
Use a question, evidence source, and outcome measure to propose a narrowly scoped QI/scholarship project.
Recognize pediatric developmental, family, and trajectory differences and their certification/training boundary.
boardDomains: Interdisciplinary Teamwork, Quality, and Professionalism (2%); published HPM curricular milestones
units.casePractice: Use the licensed pediatric serious-illness conversation case by link and develop a supervision-safe teaching plan; do not treat the guide as a validated script for every family.
units.assessment: QI one-pager plus interprofessional role/hand-off simulation.

assignment.title: Fictional serious-illness care-plan portfolio
components: A whole-person assessment and problem list for one original fictional scenario.
A 750-word goals-of-care/family-meeting plan that includes uncertainty, values questions, interdisciplinary roles, and documentation elements.
A transition/handoff checklist distinguishing general palliative care from Medicare hospice-benefit rules.
A 1-page evidence appraisal or QI proposal using a published source.
assignment.safetyRules: No real patient records, identifying details, images, orders, dosing, treatment advice, or claims of clinical competence. Cases must be fictional unless linked externally with the stated license/permission; linked materials are not to be copied or rehosted.
assignment.rubric: 40% whole-person reasoning; 25% communication/ethics; 20% evidence accuracy and citation; 15% systems/teamwork. Educational feedback is not a clinical competency determination.

formative: Unit knowledge checks using the ten original questions below.
Simulated communication script reviewed against the HPM milestones.
assessment.summative: Portfolio plus a 40-question original/open-book quiz blueprinted approximately to the published ABIM category weights. It is not an ABIM, ABFM, ABP, ACGME, or Johns Hopkins assessment and cannot validate readiness or competence.
assessment.passingClaim: No passing score, credential, credit, or board-passing prediction is offered.

studyHours.interpretation: Plan only. The 37.30 video hours are observed public recordings. Remaining hours are suggested self-study time and do not equal supervised fellowship time, clinical rotations, or protected didactics.

It does not provide a named rotation-by-rotation schedule.

boardNames: American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) Hospice and Palliative Medicine Certification Program
American Board of Family Medicine (ABFM) Certificate of Added Qualification in Hospice and Palliative Medicine
American Board of Pediatrics (ABP) Hospice and Palliative Medicine Certification
medical.boardStatus: HPM has an ABMS multi-board certification program. ABIM administers the shared examination for ABIM diplomates and specified qualifying boards; ABFM and ABP publish their own primary-board-specific eligibility and maintenance requirements. The ABIM public blueprint is used as a transparent content map, not as proprietary exam content or a promise that any particular question will appear.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Independent study, videos, readings, cases, and planned clips do not satisfy ACGME/RCPSC/CMQ fellowship training, direct observation, competency attestation, prior primary-board certification, unrestricted licensure, application, examination, or primary-board policies. ABIM policy requires prior relevant board certification, a valid unrestricted license, successful completion of formal training, competence, and the examination; its training pathway requires 12 months of full-time clinical HPM fellowship training. Practice pathways closed after 2012. ABFM requires maintained family medicine certification, at least 12 months full-time ACGME HPM fellowship, and its exam. ABP requires maintained ABP certification, valid unrestricted U.S./territory/Canada licensure, and one year of accredited HPM fellowship. Policies can change; applicants must consult their primary board.

officialProgrammes.name: Hospice and Palliative Medicine Fellowship Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official listing: ACGME accredited, one year. The education page describes a 12-month clinical fellowship with Adult and Pediatric tracks, rotations at different facilities/similar locations, interdisciplinary teams, weekly seminar, faculty supervision, and a scholarly project. It does not provide a named rotation-by-rotation schedule.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The declared packet identifies one Johns Hopkins programme. This entry researches that one actual fellowship. Johns Hopkins publicly describes Adult and Pediatric tracks inside its 12-month HPM fellowship; they are retained as institution variants within this single specialty entry, not invented as separate programmes, certificates, or duplicate catalogue entries. The public pages do not publish a month-by-month rotation schedule, named rotation sites, case volume, or a complete didactic inventory; none is inferred.
sourceCaveats: All public webpages and platform metadata were read/checked on 2026-10-07. Policies, guidelines, streaming access, and programme information can change.
ABIM blueprint percentages describe a published examination content map; they are not an official course accreditation standard, protected question disclosure, or guarantee of exam coverage.
The institutional programme page does not disclose full rotation schedules, clinical volumes, or all didactics. ACGME requirements should not be misread as a public Johns Hopkins schedule.
Free-to-view does not mean permission to rehost. All video and case links remain at original sources; no protected downloads, proprietary questions, payments, or patient records were used.
The user outline concerns nuclear medicine and imaging; it is unrelated to this HPM entry and its unsupported imaging/case-volume claims were not imported.

practiceQuestions.stem: A physician wants initial HPM certification through the ABIM training pathway. Which statement is required by the published ABIM policy?

options.text: A 12-month, full-time clinical HPM fellowship in an ACGME-, RCPSC-, or CMQ-accredited program is required.
Attendance at 36 hours of independent video study substitutes for fellowship.
Practice experience alone remains a first-time pathway.
No prior board certification or license is required.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM specifies 12 months of full-time clinical HPM fellowship training and other requirements; practice pathways ended after 2012. Independent study cannot substitute.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with serious cancer wants symptom support while receiving disease-directed treatment. What is the best conceptual response?

options.text: Palliative care can only begin after hospice election.
Palliative care may be concurrent with disease-directed treatment and is based on need, not a hospice-benefit election.
Hospice and palliative care are interchangeable Medicare terms.
Symptom assessment should wait until treatment stops.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Palliative care can accompany cancer treatment. Medicare hospice has a separate certification and election framework.

practiceQuestions.stem: In an initial palliative consultation, which omission most clearly makes the assessment incomplete?

options.text: Documenting pain intensity only.
Assessing symptoms, function/capacity, cultural values, psychosocial/spiritual supports, and caregiver stressors.
Reviewing laboratory values only.
Asking the primary team to choose goals without the patient or surrogate.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The published blueprint and milestones define comprehensive assessment as more than physical symptoms, including capacity/development, culture, and supports/stressors.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes palliative sedation in this course?

options.text: A routine response to ordinary anxiety.
A context-dependent intervention considered in rare situations of symptoms refractory to available treatments, with goals and safeguards clarified.
A way to predict time of death.
A replacement for assessment of delirium or distress.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI describes palliative sedation as potentially indicated in rare refractory end-of-life situations; the HPM blueprint identifies proportional sedation under emergencies/refractory symptoms.
practiceQuestions.domain: Palliative Care Emergencies and Refractory Symptoms

practiceQuestions.stem: A family asks for home hospice information. Which fact is specific to the Medicare Part A hospice benefit rather than a general definition of palliative care?

options.text: It can address symptoms and family stress.
It requires care from a Medicare-certified hospice, terminal-illness certification with a prognosis of 6 months or less if the illness follows its normal course, and an election statement.
It can involve an interdisciplinary team.
It may include caregiver support.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CMS lists the program, certification/prognosis, and election requirements. The other features are broader palliative-care concepts.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with cancer has escalating pain without functional improvement despite repeated analgesic escalation. What is the most defensible next learning step?

options.text: Assume pain reports are unreliable.
Reassess mechanism, function, psychosocial contributors, adverse effects, and alternative multimodal approaches rather than escalating automatically.
Apply a rigid non-palliative CDC dose threshold.
Ignore substance-use risk because the patient has cancer.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI notes that repeated escalation without improvement should trigger an alternative approach; it also discusses individualized risk assessment. CDC explicitly excludes cancer-related, palliative, and end-of-life pain from its adult outpatient guideline scope.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which setting pattern is a core ACGME HPM program requirement, not a countable lecture substitute?

options.text: At least four location types including inpatient acute care, long-term care, home visits, and ambulatory practice.
Only an inpatient consult service.
Only online case conferences.
A fixed rotation schedule identical at all institutions.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME requires participating sites in at least those four location types. Lectures can augment but cannot replace supervised clinical education.

practiceQuestions.stem: During a goals-of-care discussion, which communication move best reflects the HPM milestones?

options.text: Give a precise survival date to reduce uncertainty.
Elicit what matters, acknowledge uncertainty and emotion, summarize, make a goal-concordant recommendation, and arrange follow-up.
Avoid emotions to keep the meeting efficient.
Ask only the clinician to identify trade-offs.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The milestones emphasize responding to emotion, communicating prognosis with uncertainty, eliciting values, shared decision-making, documentation, and follow-up.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about the Johns Hopkins offering is supported by its public education page?

options.text: It is a 12-month clinical fellowship with Adult and Pediatric tracks, weekly seminar, clinical rotations at different facilities, and a scholarly project.
It publicly guarantees a named month-by-month rotation schedule.
It is an online course that replaces rotations.
Adult and pediatric tracks are publicly identified as separate ABMS certificates.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Johns Hopkins publicly describes those features. It does not publish the asserted schedule or separate certificate claim.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately preserves the pediatric HPM certification boundary?

options.text: Any video learner may take the ABP subspecialty exam.
ABP candidates need maintained ABP certification, valid unrestricted U.S./territory/Canada license, and a year in an accredited HPM fellowship, subject to ABP policy.
Pediatric exposure is excluded from HPM learning.
The HPM certification automatically follows a pediatric residency.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABP publishes those admission requirements. The ABIM blueprint notes pediatric topics may appear, but it does not confer eligibility.

title: Integrative Medicine Educator Fellowship
level: Non-ACGME clinical physician fellowship; independent postgraduate self-study curriculum-aligned independent study

prerequisites.officialFellowshipApplicantContext: CHA: family medicine physicians licensed or eligible for Massachusetts licensure. Consult CHA for current employment/application details.
prerequisites.independentStudyEntry: For physicians or supervised health-professions educators; unlicensed learners must not use it for patient management.

objectives: Define integrative/complementary/alternative/whole-person health precisely.
Construct evidence-informed patient-centered plans that preserve conventional care.
Appraise evidence, harms, interactions, quality, and applicability.
Use calibrated language for lifestyle, mind-body, nutritional, manual, and whole-system approaches.
Apply pain evidence and shared decision making without unsupervised treatment advice.
Teach residents with aligned objectives, assessment, feedback, and source transparency.
Recognize ethics, equity, referral, credentialing, and scope boundaries.

units.title: Scope, terminology, and whole-person assessment
objectives: Distinguish complementary, alternative, and integrative health without treating labels as evidence.
Build a biopsychosocial-environmental problem representation.
units.casePractice: Fictional primary-care vignette: separate goals, social context, conventional care, and possible complementary approaches.
units.assessment: One-page assessment map plus uncertainty statement.

units.title: Evidence appraisal, causal claims, and risk communication
objectives: Appraise question, design, comparator, bias, applicability, and outcome importance.
Avoid converting a mechanism or case report into a treatment claim.
units.casePractice: Appraise the linked consented case only for causal limits, co-interventions, and applicability.
units.assessment: Critical-appraisal worksheet and 150-word patient-facing uncertainty explanation.

units.title: Nutrition, lifestyle, prevention, environment, and equity
objectives: Link lifestyle/social context to measurable patient-chosen goals.
Recognize access, culture, and environment as care context rather than assumptions.
units.casePractice: Fictional chronic-pain case with shift work and food-access barriers.
units.assessment: Shared-decision behavior plan plus equity reflection.

units.title: Supplements, botanicals, quality, and interaction safety
objectives: Elicit product, dose, source, goal, medicines, and context.
Recognize when pharmacist/clinician review is needed.
units.casePractice: Fictional medicine/supplement list; find missing safety information.
units.assessment: Medication-supplement reconciliation and evidence/quality checklist.

units.title: Mind-body practice, spirituality, and meaning
objectives: Use balanced evidence and adverse-effect language for mind-body practice.
Elicit spiritual/meaning concerns without imposing beliefs.
units.casePractice: Role-play neutral discussion of meditation preference, risks, and referral boundaries.
units.assessment: Communication rubric focused on non-coercion and safety.

units.title: Complementary modalities and whole medical systems
objectives: Compare evidence, contraindications, credentialing, and referral questions.
Avoid treating cultural descriptions as proof of efficacy or safety.
units.casePractice: Create safe-referral due-diligence checklist.
units.assessment: Comparative modality brief with “unknown” column.

units.title: Integrated chronic-pain and behavioral-health care
objectives: Explain limits of nonpharmacologic options in multimodal care.
Use function-focused, coordinated, patient-centered communication.
units.casePractice: Appraise chronic-pain cohort then design fictional shared-decision conversation, not a treatment order.
units.assessment: Evidence table, functional-goal plan, and escalation criteria.

units.title: Clinical integration across populations and conditions
objectives: Transfer evidence-appraisal/coordination skills across age and comorbidity.
Avoid generalizing evidence across patients and conditions.
units.casePractice: Compare fictional vignettes with same symptom but different context.
units.assessment: Short-answer transfer exercise with citations.

units.title: Interprofessional practice, ethics, equity, and systems
objectives: Design coordinated workflows and explicit roles.
Address access, privacy, conflicts, scope, documentation, and referral.
units.casePractice: Map fictional clinic workflow for product documentation and referral.
units.assessment: Systems map and ethics memo.

units.title: Clinician educator: curriculum, teaching, assessment, and scholarship
objectives: Write observable objectives and aligned teaching/assessment.
Teach evidence appraisal without representing independent study as fellowship training.
units.casePractice: Build and peer-review a 20-minute resident session using fictional case.
units.assessment: Microteaching, rubric, learner feedback, and revision memo.

assignment.title: Evidence-to-education portfolio
deliverables: fictional whole-person map
two structured evidence appraisals
medicine/supplement safety workflow
20-minute source-annotated microteaching plan/rubric/revision
access/scope reflection
assignment.rules: Use fictional cases or linked lawful sources only; do not upload patient records, scans, or copyrighted images. All clinical claims require sources and uncertainty language.

assessment.boundary: Educational only; not CHA, Dundee, ABPS, or ABOIM assessment and not a passing predictor.

studyHours.note: 36 video hours is a target. Only 17.304167 ready hours are verified; 18.695833 planned hours are not counted.

Clinical rotations, patient visits, procedures, and self-study are not lecture hours.

The newly added long event recordings have NIH event-list duration evidence; the SPA text fetch did not expose runtime, and no time-based playback probe was performed. practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient uses acupuncture together with prescribed physical therapy. Which term best describes that arrangement?

options.text: Alternative care
Complementary care
Integrative health solely because two services exist
Evidence-free care

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCCIH calls a non-mainstream approach complementary when used together with conventional medicine. Integrative health adds coordinated, whole-person, multimodal care.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional clinician recommends a “natural” supplement without asking about medicines. What is the best first educational action?

options.text: Assume natural products are safe
Ask about all medicines/supplements, product details, and context; seek appropriate review
Stop every prescription medicine
Assume the label proves effectiveness

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCCIH and FDA warn that supplements may interact with medicines and labels do not prove effectiveness. This tests reconciliation and escalation, not treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional resident treats one published case report as proof that a multimodal intervention caused recovery. What is the strongest critique?

options.text: A favorable case proves causation
Case reports cannot give clinical detail
Co-interventions, natural history, selection, and no comparator prevent confident causal inference
Only laboratory studies may be discussed

practiceQuestions.rationale: A single case can generate hypotheses but cannot disentangle co-interventions or establish comparative effectiveness. The linked report calls for further research.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient reports anxiety after starting mindfulness. Which response best reflects the evidence/safety framing?

options.text: Mindfulness has no possible adverse effects
Stop all mental-health care
Acknowledge, assess safety/context, and coordinate appropriate support
Say the experience proves it is working

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCCIH notes generally low risks but reported negative experiences and incomplete safety evidence.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional learner says acupuncture is safe because needles are small. What correction is accurate?

options.text: Technique does not matter
Improper delivery can cause serious effects; FDA requires sterile single-use needles
Acupuncture is always contraindicated for pain
Evidence removes infection-control requirements

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCCIH describes rare serious complications from nonsterile needles/improper treatment and the FDA device requirement.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which fictional outpatient chronic-pain framing is consistent with CDC’s guideline summary?

options.text: The guideline is an inflexible law
It supports informed patient-centered decisions and does not replace individualized judgment
Every patient needs the same nonpharmacologic option
Function should not be discussed

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC calls the guideline recommendations and explicitly says it does not replace individualized clinical judgment.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which design best matches CBME for supplement safety?

options.text: Lecture without outcome or assessment
Observable objective, reconciliation exercise, feedback, and aligned rubric
Attendance only
Commercial product demonstration

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAMC describes CBME as outcomes-based and based on competencies/observable abilities.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient asks about a botanical after online claims. Which shared-decision statement is best?

options.text: It works because many people use it
There is nothing to discuss
Let’s review known/unknown evidence, harms/interactions, alternatives, and what matters to you
You must use it

practiceQuestions.rationale: Shared decision making combines evidence with patient preferences, beliefs, and values and discusses harms and consequences.

practiceQuestions.stem: A prospective two-week multimodal chronic-pain programme is single-arm. What conclusion is appropriate?

options.text: Every modality caused the outcome
It can describe associations/feasibility, but no control and multimodality limit causal attribution
It has no educational value
It replaces comparative research

practiceQuestions.rationale: The source explicitly reports observational, no-control, multimodal, selection, and follow-up limitations.

options.text: It creates board eligibility and license
It replaces residency
It is not an approved fellowship; public eligibility includes multiple requirements beyond fellowship completion
No written exam is required

boardNames: American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) — Internal Medicine Certification Examination
medical.boardStatus: ABIM is the relevant general-IM certifying board. Mapping uses the public initial CERT blueprint. January 2026 MOC/LKA blueprint is separate maintenance-assessment context, not initial-CERT eligibility. ACGME sets GME standards; it is not a certifying board.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: No course activity, video, quiz, case, or planned clip confers ABIM eligibility, ACGME credit, residency completion, licensure, procedure competence or certification. ABIM policy checked 2026-10-07: requisite predoctoral education; 36 calendar months qualifying U.S./Canadian ACGME/RCPSC/CMQ GME by Aug. 31 of exam year, including at least 30 clinical months; at least 24 months direct patient responsibility and 6 direct-care months in R-1; procedure/clinical competence and licensure/procedural requirements; programme-director verification; and passing the exam. Fellow time cannot meet IM residency training. Current application-time policy controls. Verify accreditation in ACGME public search.

officialProgrammes.name: Internal Medicine Residency
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: CHA describes a three-year 2+4 schedule (2 ambulatory weeks alternating with 4 other experiences), plus a 2026–27 one-6-week ambulatory-long-block pilot. PGY2/3 ambulatory subspecialties include cardiology, endocrine, GI, heme-onc, ID, neuro, pulmonary and rheumatology. Tuesday School is a protected weekly four-hour inpatient block, not a public video set; rotations/didactics are not lecture-hour credit.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional 34-year-old has cough for 4 days after rhinorrhea, normal vital signs, no focal lung findings, and yellow sputum. What is the best next reasoning step?

options.text: Yellow sputum establishes bacterial bronchitis.
Give routine antibiotics after 72 hours.
Evaluate for pneumonia using overall findings; colored sputum alone does not establish bacterial infection.
Obtain chest radiography in every adult with cough.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC says colored sputum does not indicate bacterial infection; evaluate acute bronchitis by looking for pneumonia risk/findings.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult has nasal discharge and daytime cough for 12 days without improvement. Which feature matches a CDC pattern supporting consideration of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis?

options.text: Any cough for 48 hours.
Persistent symptoms for more than 10 days without improvement.
Yellow mucus alone.
Normal examination after improvement.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC lists persistent symptoms >10 days without improvement, severe symptoms, or worsening after improvement.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional hospitalized adult with suspected infection becomes hypotensive and confused. What is the appropriate educational action?

options.text: Finish the module before notifying anyone.
Treat as potential sepsis emergency: promptly evaluate/escalate under facility policy and reassess.
Wait for cultures before contacting a clinician.
Assume uncomplicated bronchitis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC calls sepsis a medical emergency and directs prompt evaluation/treatment under facility policy, alerting the team and frequent reassessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient asks if stroke prevention is identical for every AF pattern. What best matches the cited guideline?

options.text: Decide only by AF pattern.
Individualize using stroke risk, bleeding risk, preferences and periodic reassessment.
Never consider kidney function.
Use a lecture title as the decision rule.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AF guideline frames stroke reduction around risk, bleeding, preferences and reassessment; AF pattern alone does not determine it.

practiceQuestions.stem: Before applying a prevention recommendation to a fictional clinic panel, what should be checked first?

options.text: Last year’s slide only.
A current authoritative recommendation for population, net benefit, exceptions and update date.
A social-media summary.
The same screening for every adult.

practiceQuestions.rationale: USPSTF guidance is population-specific and must be date-checked.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional 52-year-old has never had an HIV test and is in routine care. Which approach is consistent with CDC guidance?

options.text: Routine opt-out testing subject to law/setting, with linkage planning.
Test only after disclosure of stigmatized risk.
Do not test without symptoms.
Use results without linkage planning.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC recommends routine testing ages 13–64, opt-out framing, and linkage to prevention/care.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult with CKD receives a new discharge medication list. What is the safest study deliverable?

options.text: Issue a patient-specific dose change.
Create a reconciliation question list flagging kidney function, indication, monitoring and missing data for a supervising clinician.
Ignore renal function.
Copy a dosing table into a chart.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The course practices safety reasoning, not prescribing; patient-specific decisions require authorized care.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional 69-year-old asks about breast-cancer screening. Which statement appears on the USPSTF A/B listing?

options.text: Biennial mammography for women aged 40–74.
No screening before age 75.
Screen only by race.
A webpage replaces shared discussion.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The listing reports a grade B biennial mammography recommendation for women 40–74.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional discharge case includes opioid use disorder, unstable housing and new follow-up needs. What skill is appropriate?

options.text: A stigma-free SBAR handoff naming responsibilities, preferences and escalation contacts.
Omit goals and social barriers.
Authorize controlled-substance treatment independently.
Post a real discharge summary.

practiceQuestions.rationale: TeamSTEPPS provides teamwork/communication tools; this course does not authorize treatment or disclosure.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional learner wants an LIDC-IDRI CT image in a public slide deck. What must happen?

options.text: Strip attribution.
Use under CC BY 3.0, cite the collection DOI/data citation, and never attempt re-identification.
Call it synthetic.
Add an identifier.

practiceQuestions.rationale: TCIA lists CC BY 3.0 and requires data citation; policy prohibits identifying/contacting participants.

title: Interventional Pulmonology Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (actual combined institutional programme; independent-study companion is nonclinical)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.level: Advanced postgraduate pulmonary/critical-care knowledge; intended for physicians-in-training or clinicians studying concepts under appropriate local supervision.
knowledge: Adult thoracic anatomy and pulmonary physiology.
Foundational pulmonary/critical-care medicine, lung cancer staging concepts, pleural disease, safe-sedation principles, and evidence appraisal.
Ability to interpret peer-reviewed/guideline language and to recognize scope-of-practice limits.
hardBoundaries: No learner may perform, direct, or advise a real procedure from this course.
Learners needing clinical competence require accredited training, simulation, direct supervision, local privileging, and applicable licensure.
AABIP applicant prerequisites are certifier-specific and are not met by this curriculum.

objectives: Use the published AABIP blueprint to organize IP disease-specific and procedural knowledge without representing it as a guarantee of examination success.

Explain diagnostic and multidisciplinary reasoning for thoracic malignancy, EBUS-TBNA specimen handling, central-airway problems, pleural disease, benign lung disease, and selected therapeutic interventions.
Apply current publicly cited limits: CHEST 2024 EBUS-TBNA handling, FDA’s bounded Zephyr valve indication, and GINA 2026 thermoplasty caution.
Distinguish educational video viewing, image review, and simulated reasoning from procedural competence and patient care.
State current AABIP versus ABIM certification boundaries accurately and use lawful, de-identified image data with attribution.

units.title: Scope, safety culture, and multidisciplinary decision-making
objectives: Distinguish diagnostic reasoning from supervised procedural competence.
Construct a multidisciplinary referral question and escalation plan for an airway, pleural, or nodule problem.
topics: IP scope; consent and patient-centered goals; team roles; complication anticipation; referral thresholds
units.casePractice: Write a de-identified, fictional MDT referral note; identify information that cannot be inferred from imaging alone.
units.assessment: 10-item safety/role quiz and faculty-style self-audit using a checklist.

units.title: Airway anatomy, physiology, anesthesia, and procedural preparation
objectives: Relate airway obstruction physiology and ventilation choices to procedural risk.
Explain why sedation/anesthesia planning requires local protocols and a qualified team.
topics: central-airway anatomy; jet ventilation concepts; oxygenation; monitoring; moderate/deep sedation; local anesthesia
units.casePractice: Map a fictional pre-procedure risk screen to team roles; do not create medication orders.
units.assessment: Short-answer safety rationale plus 5 blueprint-mapped items.

units.title: Thoracic oncology, lung nodules, and diagnostic strategy
objectives: Frame a peripheral nodule or mediastinal target as a diagnostic question rather than a device-selection exercise.
Describe how staging, molecular testing needs, and multidisciplinary care constrain specimen strategy.
topics: screening; pretest probability; staging; target selection; specimen adequacy; molecular/immune markers; shared decision-making
boardDomains: Disease Specific Knowledge—thoracic malignancy (11.1%); diagnostic approaches to peripheral nodule (7.4%)
units.casePractice: Use a TCIA collection only as a research-image review: record target location and uncertainty, then state why no real-patient decision follows.
units.assessment: Case-interpretation worksheet; answers are reasoning hypotheses, not diagnoses or treatment plans.

units.title: Convex/radial EBUS and EBUS-TBNA specimen stewardship
objectives: Identify the parts of a source-guided EBUS-TBNA workflow that affect sample adequacy.
Apply the 2024 CHEST specimen-handling recommendations in a simulated workflow.
topics: linear and radial EBUS; nodal stations; needle choice; passes; ROSE; cytology and molecular pathways; communication with pathology
boardDomains: Procedural Knowledge—convex/radial EBUS (6.7%); Disease Specific Knowledge—thoracic malignancy (11.1%)
units.casePractice: Create a fictional specimen-routing flowchart for a suspected malignancy, citing the guideline; no procedural performance.
units.assessment: Single-best-answer quiz plus documented rationale for needle/passes and pathology handoff.

units.title: Navigation, robotic bronchoscopy, and cone-beam CT: evidence-aware use
objectives: Compare navigation, robotic, and cone-beam CT as adjunctive approaches without claiming universal superiority.
Recognize radiation, access, yield, and complication questions that require local credentialing and multidisciplinary review.
topics: peripheral access; imaging adjuncts; radiation awareness; diagnostic yield interpretation; device-neutral appraisal
boardDomains: Procedural Knowledge—navigational/robotic/cone-beam bronchoscopy (7.4%); diagnostic peripheral nodule (7.4%)
units.casePractice: Critique a fictional technology proposal with an evidence, safety, conflict-of-interest, and access checklist.
units.assessment: Structured evidence appraisal; no device training sign-off.

units.title: Central airway obstruction, rigid bronchoscopy, dilation, and foreign-body principles
objectives: Classify malignant and nonmalignant central-airway obstruction as urgent multidisciplinary problems.
Compare the intent, limits, and complication concerns of rigid access, balloon dilation, and retrieval concepts.
topics: CAO assessment; malignant/nonmalignant causes; rigid bronchoscopy; foreign-body retrieval; balloon tracheoplasty/bronchoplasty; rescue planning
boardDomains: Disease Specific Knowledge—malignant CAO (5.2%) and nonmalignant CAO (3.0%); Procedural Knowledge—rigid/foreign body (5.9%), balloon procedures (3.7%)
units.casePractice: Prepare a fictional airway-obstruction MDT agenda emphasizing urgency, surgical/anesthesia input, and alternatives.
units.assessment: Algorithm critique with red-flag escalation rather than a technical maneuver test.

units.title: Ablation, stents, fistulas, and therapeutic bronchoscopy limits
objectives: Differentiate categories of endobronchial ablative therapy and stenting from a claim of individual competence.
Explain why stent selection and follow-up require patient-specific risk-benefit assessment and specialist follow-up.
topics: electrocautery; APC; laser; cryotherapy; PDT; brachytherapy; stents; airway-esophageal and bronchopleural fistulas; complications
boardDomains: Procedural Knowledge—ablation (5.9%), tracheobronchial stents (5.9%); Disease Specific Knowledge—CAO and pleural/fistula topics
units.casePractice: Compare two fictional airway-device plans in a benefits/harms/alternatives table; cite the reading rather than a manufacturer claim.
units.assessment: Written reasoning assessment; pass requires explicit referral and follow-up safeguards.

units.title: Pleural disease, ultrasound, thoracentesis, IPCs, pleurodesis, and thoracoscopy
objectives: Organize malignant and nonmalignant pleural problems into diagnostic, symptom, lung-expandability, and goals-of-care questions.
Explain what the ATS/STS/STR MPE guideline is for and what it does not replace.
topics: thoracic ultrasound; thoracentesis; tube thoracostomy; tunneled pleural catheter; pleurodesis; medical thoracoscopy; pleural biopsy; infection/empyema
boardDomains: Disease Specific Knowledge—pleural diseases (6.7%); Procedural Knowledge—pleural procedures (8.1%)
units.casePractice: Use a fictional symptom-and-lung-expansion scenario to make a guideline-linked comparison table; do not prescribe care.
units.assessment: Annotated MPE decision map and 8-question quiz.

units.title: Benign lung disease, cryobiopsy, transplant airways, and hemoptysis
objectives: State the diagnostic purpose and safety constraints of transbronchial cryobiopsy.
Identify when hemoptysis, transplant-airway, or benign-disease questions require urgent specialist and institutional pathways.
topics: ILD; cryobiopsy; sarcoidosis; infection; transplant anastomoses; massive hemoptysis; multidisciplinary pathology/radiology review
boardDomains: Disease Specific Knowledge—benign lung disease (0.7%), transplant complications (2.2%); CHEST cryobiopsy guideline scope
units.casePractice: Draft a fictional pre-procedure uncertainty list that distinguishes evidence review from performing cryobiopsy.
units.assessment: Safety-boundary vignette assessment.

units.title: Bronchoscopic lung-volume reduction and bronchial thermoplasty
objectives: Describe the FDA’s specific Zephyr-valve indication without extending it to unselected COPD.
State GINA’s limited-evidence/registry framing for bronchial thermoplasty.
topics: severe emphysema; hyperinflation; collateral ventilation; BLVR; severe asthma; thermoplasty; selection limits; longitudinal follow-up
boardDomains: Disease Specific Knowledge—endoscopic therapeutic COPD (2.2%); Procedural Knowledge—thermoplasty/BLVR (1.5%)
units.casePractice: Create a fictional eligibility-exclusion checklist that quotes the FDA/GINA wording and labels all local criteria as out of scope.
units.assessment: 5-item indication/limitation quiz.

units.title: Quality, ethics, coding, evidence appraisal, and practice boundaries
objectives: Interpret the published AABIP blueprint as a study map, not protected exam content or a guarantee of passing.
Explain reporting, conflict-of-interest, quality, palliative-care, and coding boundaries without providing billing advice.
topics: biostatistics; outcomes; quality improvement; ethics; palliative care; coding/billing awareness; conflicts; AI claims
boardDomains: Disease Specific Knowledge—ethics/palliative care (3.0%) and biostatistics (0.7%); Procedural Knowledge—coding/billing (0.7%)
units.casePractice: Appraise a fictional device presentation for evidence quality, sponsorship, and missing safety outcomes.
units.assessment: Evidence-and-ethics reflection plus original MCQs.

units.title: Integration, AABIP blueprint review, and supervised-training boundaries
objectives: Synthesize a multidisciplinary plan for a fictional thoracic intervention question while naming uncertainty and referral needs.
Accurately state AABIP versus ABIM/ABMS status and the limits of independent study.
topics: blueprint integration; AABIP eligibility; ACGME/AABIP accreditation; ABIM ongoing evaluation; competency versus knowledge; portfolio review
boardDomains: All AABIP blueprint domains; emphasis on disease-specific (50.4%) and procedural knowledge (49.6%)
units.casePractice: Complete a capstone fictional MDT case packet and a limitations statement; no logbook, credential, or sign-off is awarded.
units.assessment: Cumulative 40-item original self-assessment and structured capstone rubric.

assignment.title: Fictional multidisciplinary interventional-pulmonology case portfolio
deliverables: Three de-identified/fictitious case-reasoning worksheets (nodule/EBUS, central airway, and pleural/BLVR-or-asthma boundary).

practiceQuestions.stem: A study plan claims that watching public procedure videos is equivalent to being cleared to perform EBUS. Which response is best?

options.text: Accept it if all nodal stations are viewed.
Accept it after a self-reported number of views.
Reject the equivalence: AABIP describes videos as a supplement to simulation and supervised mentorship, not a substitute.
Accept it when the viewer has read the exam blueprint.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AABIP explicitly states its procedure videos are educational and not a substitute for mentored hands-on training. Observing a video does not demonstrate procedural competency or confer credentials.

practiceQuestions.stem: In the 2024 CHEST EBUS-TBNA specimen guideline, which approach is suggested for suspected malignant disease?

options.text: Three or fewer passes only.
Four or more needle passes.
Never use ROSE.
Always use a 19-gauge needle.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CHEST’s guideline-in-focus page states a suggestion for four or more rather than three or fewer passes in suspected malignancy. It also presents separate recommendations on ROSE and needle size; this does not authorize unsupervised procedure performance.

practiceQuestions.stem: For suspected malignant disease undergoing EBUS-TBNA, what needle-size comparison does CHEST’s 2024 summary make?

options.text: Prefer 21- or 22-gauge over 19-gauge.
Prefer 19-gauge over any smaller needle.
Require 25-gauge for every sample.
Needle size is not addressed.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline summary suggests a smaller 21- or 22-gauge needle over a 19-gauge needle for suspected malignant disease. The choice belongs within a supervised, patient-specific process.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult has severe emphysema and hyperinflation. Which additional condition is in the FDA approval-order indication for the Zephyr Endobronchial Valve System?

options.text: Any asthma phenotype.
Little to no collateral ventilation in the target lung regions.
A positive PET scan.
All COPD regardless of emphysema or hyperinflation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The FDA approval order specifies adult patients with hyperinflation associated with severe emphysema in lung regions with little to no collateral ventilation. It is not a general COPD or asthma indication.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best reflects the 2026 GINA severe-asthma guide on bronchial thermoplasty?

options.text: It is first-line therapy for all asthma.
It can be considered with registry enrollment, but efficacy and long-term safety evidence are limited.
It replaces inhaled corticosteroids.
It has no role in any circumstance.

practiceQuestions.rationale: GINA frames bronchial thermoplasty as a consideration with registry enrollment and notes limited efficacy and long-term safety evidence. This supports careful specialist evaluation, not a blanket recommendation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which two top-level domains make up the published AABIP IP Board Exam Blueprint?

options.text: Pulmonary physiology and radiology only.
Disease Specific Knowledge and Procedural Knowledge.
Research and administration only.
Pediatrics and geriatrics.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The published blueprint divides content into Disease Specific Knowledge (50.4%) and Procedural Knowledge (49.6%). The blueprint is a public study map, not protected exam content and not a passing guarantee.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which condition is required in the current AABIP accredited-fellowship pathway for initial IP Board Certification?

options.text: Completion of any online course.
Successful completion of an accredited IP fellowship, with program-director attestation and training certificate.
A self-created procedure log only.
ABIM IP certification.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AABIP’s 2026 application describes accredited-fellowship completion, a program-director attestation letter, and a fellowship certificate; it states procedure logs are not required for that pathway. This independent course confers none of these.

practiceQuestions.stem: As of the ABIM Pulmonary Disease Board’s July 2026 summary, what is the most accurate statement about ABIM IP certification?

options.text: An ABIM IP exam is already available to all course completers.
ABIM is still evaluating potential development and practice-pathway options; Board consideration needs additional data.
AABIP certification has been replaced by ABIM certification.
No organization offers an IP certification examination.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM reported ongoing evaluation and potential development, including an Intent to Certify survey and data for Board consideration. AABIP separately administers its own IP Board Certification process.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner selects the LIDC-IDRI CT collection for a noncommercial, de-identified image-review exercise. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: It contains synthetic CT images with no attribution requirement.
It contains authentic thoracic CT and annotations and is listed CC BY 3.0 with data citation required.
It is a live patient record system.
It creates procedural privileges.

practiceQuestions.rationale: TCIA describes LIDC-IDRI as thoracic CT with radiologist annotations, lists CC BY 3.0 and requires data citation. It is a research/education resource, not clinical decision support or a competency record.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional learner wants to call the BIDMC page a generic directory category rather than a fellowship. What is the best correction?

options.text: It is only a directory label and gives no programme identity.
It describes an actual Harvard Combined BIDMC-MGH IP Fellowship, while omitting a granular rotation calendar and procedure volumes.
It is a nuclear medicine fellowship.
It guarantees ABIM IP eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: BIDMC identifies a combined BIDMC-MGH fellowship and its application prerequisite. Its public page does not publish a detailed rotation calendar or case-volume targets; those must not be invented.

title: Osler Medical Residency Training Program
prerequisites: Advanced learner level: prior core biomedical sciences and supervised clinical-clerkship exposure or equivalent foundational study are strongly recommended.
Ability to interpret common clinical vocabulary, vital signs, basic laboratory units, ECG terminology, and primary guideline documents.
For any real patient question, use a licensed supervising clinician and local protocols. Do not enter, upload, or discuss real protected health information in course work.
No prerequisite is a substitute for medical-school, residency, licensure, or institutional onboarding requirements.
objectives: Build prioritized problem representations and mechanism-based differentials across adult Internal Medicine.
Use dated primary guidance and evidence resources while naming uncertainty, population limits, and supervision boundaries.
Interpret the ABIM CERT blueprint as an assessment specification, not as proof of readiness or eligibility.
Connect inpatient, ambulatory, prevention, safety, communication, and equity questions in fictional educational cases.
Recognize when a question needs urgent clinical assessment, specialty consultation, local policy, or supervised procedural care.

units.title: Clinical reasoning, diagnostic safety and high-value inpatient care
objectives: Construct a concise problem representation and a prioritized, mechanism-based differential.
Choose data that change probability or management, and name uncertainty and diagnostic-safety follow-up.
Reconcile medications and handoffs without treating an electronic record as ground truth.
boardDomains: ABIM CERT cross-cutting: Clinical Epidemiology; Patient Safety; Ethics; health equity
casePractice: Use the linked de-identified medication-reconciliation exercise as a process case; do not enter any real EHR.
Write a one-sentence representation and three-item differential for a fictional admission.
units.assessment: Submit a diagnostic time-out and a reconciliation discrepancy log; facilitator/self-key checks for evidence, uncertainty, and escalation.

units.title: Cardiovascular disease, atrial fibrillation and thromboembolic reasoning
objectives: Separate rhythm diagnosis, stroke-risk estimation, bleeding considerations, and shared decision-making in a fictional AF vignette.
Interpret an ASCVD-risk-reduction discussion without confusing risk calculators with automatic orders.
Recognize when chest-pain/dyspnea imaging reasoning needs urgent supervised evaluation.
boardDomains: ABIM CERT cross-cutting: Clinical Epidemiology; Ethics
casePractice: Linked Radiopaedia pulmonary-emboli case: first use hidden-diagnosis mode, then compare the stated findings; no local image export.
Linked aortic-dissection case: identify the stated true/false lumen description and list escalation questions.
units.assessment: One-page evidence map: presenting syndrome → dangerous alternatives → information needed → guideline domain; no treatment plan for a real person.

units.title: Pulmonary disease and critical care
objectives: Compare obstructive-airway, parenchymal-lung, vascular, and extrapulmonary mechanisms of dyspnea.
State why evolving ARDS definitions and asthma strategies require date-checked source review.
Frame supportive-care, prognosis, and team-communication questions for an ICU case simulation.
boardDomains: ABIM CERT cross-cutting: Critical Care Medicine; Palliative and End-of-Life Care
casePractice: For a fictional dyspnea case, build a problem representation and specify the clinical supervisor/escalation boundary before discussing tests.
units.assessment: Five-minute oral presentation using an illness-script table and an explicit uncertainty statement.

units.title: Infectious diseases and diagnostic microbiology
objectives: Organize a syndrome-first differential for febrile illness and identify host, exposure, and device clues.
Distinguish screening, diagnostic testing, and linkage-to-care concepts for HIV without assuming any patient’s status.
Explain why a novel microbiologic result must be interpreted with pretest probability and specialist context.
boardDomains: ABIM CERT cross-cutting: Prevention; Occupational Medicine
casePractice: Create a fictional exposure timeline and separate screening from diagnostic questions; do not use a real person’s laboratory record.
units.assessment: Short answer: justify two initial information requests and two reasons not to overinterpret a single advanced test.

units.title: Endocrinology, diabetes, obesity and metabolic bone disease
objectives: Recognize endocrine presentations that need structured differential diagnosis rather than pattern matching.
Locate the current ADA standard section relevant to a diabetes question and state the date/version used.
Connect obesity, diabetes, bone health, and comorbidity assessment without offering individualized drug or dose advice.
boardDomains: ABIM CERT: Endocrinology, Diabetes, and Metabolism (9%)
casePractice: For a fictional patient, create an endocrine problem list and identify which missing history/labs would change the differential.
units.assessment: Open-book source-location task: identify the ADA sections on diagnosis, pharmacologic treatment, and CKD risk—without copying algorithms.

units.title: Nephrology, urology and medication stewardship
objectives: Use the KDIGO 2024 CKD framework as a dated reference for classification, risk assessment, complications, and medication stewardship.
Explain why CKD changes the context of cardiovascular and medication decisions but does not itself supply an individual prescription.
Identify recurrent-stone prevention questions appropriate for supervised outpatient evaluation.
casePractice: Use a fictional laboratory trend to separate chronicity, severity, and data-quality questions; do not calculate or recommend dosing.
units.assessment: Classify three fictional data sets as insufficient data, possible chronic disease, or acute change needing urgent clinical review, with rationale.

units.title: Gastroenterology and hepatology
objectives: Build a broad differential for abdominal symptoms and vascular/liver complications.
Navigate the current AASLD/IDSA HCV guidance by stage—test/evaluate/monitor, treatment-naive, special populations—rather than memorizing a static regimen.
Recognize hospital-to-outpatient coordination questions in inflammatory bowel disease.
casePractice: For a fictional positive HCV screening result, chart the verification/evaluation questions and use the current guidance landing page—not an old lecture—as the source of current instructions.
units.assessment: Write a staged information-gathering plan that labels what is known, unknown, and requires supervised interpretation.

units.title: Hematology, oncology and prevention
objectives: Distinguish risk assessment, screening, diagnostic evaluation, staging, and treatment decision roles.
Apply prevention recommendations only to the population specified by the cited guidance.
Identify oncology red flags requiring multidisciplinary and specialty input.
casePractice: Use the USPSTF index to identify the recommendation population and grade for a prevention question; do not generalize it to excluded populations.
units.assessment: Two-column exercise: label statements as screening versus diagnostic evaluation and cite the population/condition qualifier.

units.title: Neurology, psychiatry, substance use and geriatric syndromes
objectives: Compare acute versus chronic cognitive/neurologic change and state when collateral history is essential.
Use non-stigmatizing language and identify the evidence-supported medication categories for OUD as a learning exercise.
Integrate delirium risk, polypharmacy, function, and goals in a geriatric problem representation.
casePractice: Use a fictional older-adult medication list to identify potential contributors to acute confusion and the need for team/supervisor review.
units.assessment: Reflective case note using person-first language plus a safety-net statement; it is not a treatment order.

units.title: Allergy/immunology, rheumatology, orthopedics and ambulatory consultation
objectives: Differentiate inflammatory, infectious, degenerative, and medication-related explanations for systemic complaints.
Recognize that rare autoinflammatory disease and large-vessel vasculitis require phenotype, time course, and specialist context.
Identify the limits of an ENT symptom lecture within a general Internal Medicine curriculum.
casePractice: Produce a time-course table for a fictional inflammatory syndrome and list discriminating findings; do not label any sign pathognomonic.
units.assessment: Peer/self-check differential that includes at least one infectious, malignant, medication-related, and inflammatory alternative.

units.title: Women’s health, prevention, equity and ambulatory general internal medicine
objectives: Locate preventive recommendations and state the specific population, interval, and grade before applying them in a fictional case.
Explain routine opt-out HIV screening and its stigma-reducing purpose in the U.S. CDC guidance.
Identify missing board domains—obstetrics/gynecology, ophthalmology, and dental/ENT—and route them to planned supplements rather than claiming coverage.
boardDomains: ABIM CERT: Obstetrics and Gynecology (3%)—planned clip gap
ABIM CERT: Otolaryngology and Dental Medicine (1%)
casePractice: Audit a fictional preventive-care note for population qualifiers, consent/opt-out language, and access barriers.
units.assessment: Create a prevention checklist for a fictional patient, then mark every item that requires clinician confirmation of local policy or individual context.

units.title: Integration: inpatient-to-ambulatory synthesis, leadership and consultation boundaries
objectives: Synthesize multi-morbidity using a prioritized problem list, contingencies, and follow-up ownership.
State what independent study cannot replace: supervised patient care, procedures, feedback, continuity clinic, team roles, and program director assessment.
Use the official Osler rotation descriptions as context without representing them as the course’s clinical experiences.
boardDomains: All ABIM CERT domains; cross-cutting Patient Safety, Ethics, Clinical Epidemiology, Prevention, health equity
casePractice: Capstone fictional case: generate a problem list, differential, dated evidence sources, contingency triggers, and one sentence naming what requires direct supervision.
units.assessment: Faculty/peer rubric for prioritization, uncertainty, equity, safety-netting, and source quality. Passing this rubric is not a competency determination.

assignment.title: Fictional longitudinal Internal Medicine synthesis portfolio
deliverables: Twelve brief source-and-reasoning worksheets (one/unit).
Two linked, fully fictional composite cases: one inpatient dyspnea/arrhythmia presentation and one ambulatory multimorbidity/prevention visit.
A medication-reconciliation process map using only the linked de-identified MedEdPORTAL exercise or invented medication names.
A dated evidence ledger that identifies source, publication/update date where shown, population, uncertainty, and a supervision/escalation boundary.
assignment.rules: Do not use real patient data, screenshots, scans, proprietary question banks, or EHR access. No diagnosis or treatment plan for an actual person. Image cases remain on their original site and are credited/licensed as stated.

components.name: Viewing and evidence ledger
components.standard: Log each unique video ID once, its observed duration, two learning points, and whether content requires a current-source check.

components.name: Unit reasoning worksheets
components.standard: Score with a rubric for problem representation, differential breadth, evidence quality, uncertainty, safety-netting, and equity.

components.name: Original practice questions
components.standard: Complete the ten original questions and explain the source-supported rationale; these are not ABIM items or a score predictor.

components.name: Fictional capstone portfolio
components.standard: Demonstrate source-aware synthesis and state direct-supervision limits.

assessment.completionInterpretation: A suggested 70% self-assessment target identifies material for review only. It does not establish clinical competence, board eligibility, licensure, credit, accreditation, affiliation, readiness for unsupervised care, or a guarantee of passing any examination.

studyHours.note: 90-hour study plan = 40.977 verified external video hours + 20 readings + 18 case/worksheet + 11.023 portfolio/question review. Planned clips are excluded because they do not exist as verified recordings.

mapping.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / The Johns Hopkins Hospital
mapping.name: Osler Medical Residency Training Program
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: The official page describes an actual, three-year Internal Medicine residency with acute and ambulatory experiences. The public curriculum describes a 6+2 block schedule; PGY-1 general medicine, MICU/CCU, progressive care, oncology, ED, ambulatory GIM/rheumatology/endocrinology; PGY-2 subspecialty and leadership rotations; and PGY-3 supervisory general medicine/ICU/CCU/oncology/ED, ambulatory and elective/research blocks. These are clinical rotations with direct patient-care roles, not video lectures and are not counted in this course’s lecture hours.

boardNames: American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) — Internal Medicine Certification Examination
medical.boardStatus: Mapped for independent study to the ABIM Internal Medicine Certification Examination (CERT) blueprint. This mapping is educational only; it is not ABIM endorsement, an exam-prep guarantee, residency accreditation, or a certification pathway.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABIM controls certification. For the standard Internal Medicine pathway, ABIM states that candidates must meet required medical education, satisfactorily complete 36 calendar months of accredited U.S./Canadian GME by the stated deadline (including 30 clinical months), meet direct-patient-responsibility and clinical-competence requirements, meet licensure/procedural requirements, and pass the ABIM examination. The narrow ABIM Research Pathway has its own 24-month accredited categorical IM/20-month direct-care minimum plus specified research and clinical subspecialty requirements. No self-study item, video, quiz, planned clip, or course completion supplies any of those requirements or eligibility; confirm current policy directly with ABIM and a program director.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / The Johns Hopkins Hospital
officialProgrammes.name: Osler Medical Residency Training Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: The official page describes an actual, three-year Internal Medicine residency with acute and ambulatory experiences. The public curriculum describes a 6+2 block schedule; PGY-1 general medicine, MICU/CCU, progressive care, oncology, ED, ambulatory GIM/rheumatology/endocrinology; PGY-2 subspecialty and leadership rotations; and PGY-3 supervisory general medicine/ICU/CCU/oncology/ED, ambulatory and elective/research blocks. These are clinical rotations with direct patient-care roles, not video lectures and are not counted in this course’s lecture hours.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This is an actual separately named Johns Hopkins Internal Medicine residency, not a generic directory category. Transparent study scope: adult general Internal Medicine knowledge, diagnostic reasoning, inpatient/ambulatory systems, prevention, and board-blueprint domains. The user-supplied nuclear-medicine/Emory/Harvard outline is not relevant to this entry and is not imported. The Johns Hopkins pages distinguish complementary pathways (Global Health, Patient Safety & Quality, Medical Education) and tracks (Primary Care, Data Science, Physician Scientist); they are variants within or alongside the Osler residency, not separate clinical specialties, certificates, or extra board certifications. The public Osler page viewed for this entry does not itself state a current ACGME accreditation status; this entry does not independently certify accreditation or infer ABIM eligibility from directory labeling.
sourceCaveats: Official Osler curriculum pages describe real residency rotations and local recordings but do not publish a public, complete, duration-verified archive of its asynchronous sessions. Those local recordings are not claimed or counted.

The 42 counted videos are external public recordings from EVMS Medicine and UCSF Department of Medicine, selected for Internal Medicine relevance. They are not Johns Hopkins/Osler lectures, are not endorsed by Johns Hopkins or ABIM, and can change availability.
Duration evidence is playlist UI plus public flat-playlist metadata observed 2026-10-07; publication dates were unavailable in captured metadata and are null, not guessed.
Only direct source links are supplied. Do not download, rehost, paywall, embed as a substitute for source terms, or reproduce protected tables, slides, questions, images, or algorithms.
Radiopaedia cases are linked lawful educational resources under stated CC BY-NC-SA terms. They are not exported, are not complete datasets, and are not evidence for a diagnosis in any real person.
Guidelines are date-checked as of 2026-10-07 and can change. They inform study; they do not define a standard of care or replace clinician judgment/local protocol.

The supplied user outline was a nuclear medicine/radiology/Emory/Harvard outline, not evidence about the assigned Osler Internal Medicine residency. Unsupported volumes, equipment, variants, modalities, and certification claims were excluded.
