practiceQuestions.stem: A learner completes every video and quiz in this independent course. Which statement most accurately describes ABIM Internal Medicine certification eligibility?

options.text: Course completion alone establishes eligibility.
Eligibility requires the learner to self-attest to clinical skill.
ABIM requires specified accredited training, competence/other requirements, and the certification examination; self-study cannot substitute.
A public lecture ledger replaces an accredited residency year.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM—not this course—sets eligibility. Its standard pathway includes 36 calendar months of accredited GME, 30 clinical months, direct patient responsibility, clinical competence and other requirements, plus the examination.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional person with atrial fibrillation and uncertain stroke-prevention benefit, what is the best learning-framework statement?

options.text: A risk score automatically determines treatment regardless of context.
A validated risk score estimates risk, while relevant modifiers and shared decision-making may inform the clinical decision.
Bleeding considerations are never relevant.
Public lectures are sufficient to make an individual anticoagulation decision.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AF guideline describes validated risk scores as estimates and highlights risk modifiers and shared decision-making in uncertain/intermediate situations. This is an educational framing, not an individual recommendation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional 28-year-old presents for routine care and has no stated HIV-testing history. Which CDC teaching point is correct?

options.text: Only people who disclose a specific risk factor should be offered testing.
CDC recommends routine opt-out HIV testing at least once for patients ages 13–64, with more frequent testing for ongoing risk factors.
Counseling is a prerequisite for every HIV test.
A self-test detects infection earlier than a nucleic-acid test.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC recommends routine opt-out testing ages 13–64, annual testing for ongoing risk factors, and notes that prevention counseling is not a requirement for testing.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which HIV test type can detect HIV earliest after an exposure according to the cited CDC clinical guidance?

options.text: Antibody-only test
Antigen/antibody combination test
Nucleic-acid test (NAT)
All types have the same eclipse period

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC describes NATs as detecting HIV RNA and detecting infection earliest, followed by antigen/antibody tests and then antibody tests.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which option correctly distinguishes evidence-supported medication categories for opioid use disorder from a medication used only for acute withdrawal symptoms?

options.text: Lofexidine is a long-term OUD medication; methadone is only for withdrawal.
Methadone, buprenorphine, and naltrexone are FDA-approved OUD medications; lofexidine treats acute withdrawal symptoms and is not long-term OUD treatment.
No medication can reduce overdose risk.
Medication discussion removes the need for supervised assessment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NIDA identifies methadone, buprenorphine, and naltrexone as FDA-approved OUD medications and distinguishes lofexidine for acute withdrawal symptoms.

practiceQuestions.stem: For an average-risk fictional woman aged 52, which statement matches the current USPSTF A/B recommendation index cited in this course?

options.text: Biennial screening mammography is recommended for women ages 40–74 (B recommendation).
Mammography is recommended only after age 75.
Screening recommendations have no age or population qualifiers.
A learner can replace local clinical review with the index.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The USPSTF index lists biennial breast-cancer screening mammography for women aged 40–74 as a B recommendation. Individual circumstances still require clinical context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional hospital admission has three conflicting medication lists. What is the best process response?

options.text: Pick the newest list without checking it.
Copy all lists into the discharge note unchanged.
Triangulate sources, clarify discrepancies, and reconcile medications in the institution’s supervised workflow.
Use an independent-study worksheet as an actual EHR order.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The MedEdPORTAL session teaches reconciliation using multiple source lists, discrepancy clarification, and a safe training/EHR workflow. This course supplies no EHR access or permission to enter orders.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best reflects the current HCV Guidance source used in Unit 7?

options.text: A single old lecture is sufficient for all HCV decisions.
The guidance is organized around stages such as test/evaluate/monitor and patient profiles, and it reports June 2026 updates.
HCV evaluation does not require patient-specific information.
The course can independently authorize antiviral treatment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AASLD/IDSA HCV Guidance site reports June 2026 updates and provides stage/profile navigation. It is used for dated reference, not as an authorization to treat.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the most accurate dated statement about the CKD reference in this course?

options.text: KDIGO 2024 has been replaced completely by a finished focused update.
KDIGO states its 2024 CKD guideline remains the current global standard while a focused Chapter 3 update is under way.
CKD guidance removes the need to examine a patient.
A study course can calculate and prescribe all renal medication dosing.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The KDIGO page expressly states that the 2024 guideline remains current and that a focused Chapter 3 update is in progress.

practiceQuestions.stem: A slide author wants to copy the entire current GINA report into a public course website. What is the appropriate course-design response?

options.text: Copy it because it is freely downloadable.
Link to the official report and respect GINA’s stated copyright/distribution restrictions.
Replace it with an unverified summary from a lecture.
Claim it provides a local clinical protocol.

practiceQuestions.rationale: GINA provides a free PDF but states that copies may not be distributed or posted without authorization. This course links to it and uses original summaries.

title: Rheumatology Fellowship
prerequisites: For the real BIDMC fellowship: three years of Internal Medicine or Family Medicine residency before fellowship start, per BIDMC; applicants should consult current programme/ERAS requirements.

For this independent study: prior core Internal Medicine knowledge; basic clinical epidemiology; ability to read guidelines critically; and access to a licensed clinician/educator for any discussion of real clinical cases.
This self-study does not permit independent arthrocentesis, injection, ultrasound interpretation, diagnosis, prescribing, or treatment changes.
objectives: Build a safety-first differential for acute and chronic musculoskeletal complaints.
Integrate history, examination, laboratory, imaging, pathology, and synovial-fluid evidence in context.
Recognize inflammatory arthritis, connective-tissue disease, vasculitis, crystal disease, myositis, and common mimics.
Identify potential organ-threatening features requiring urgent supervised evaluation.
Use current guideline sources critically and distinguish recommendations from individualized care.
Explain ABIM/ACGME/BIDMC training and certification boundaries accurately.
Appraise genuine de-identified image/case resources while honoring licensing and privacy rules.
Communicate a differential, uncertainty, escalation plan, and multidisciplinary roles in a consult-style format.

units.title: Immunology, inflammation, and the rheumatologic consultation
objectives: Connect innate/adaptive immune mechanisms to inflammatory phenotypes.
Frame a problem representation that separates inflammatory, mechanical, infectious, malignant, metabolic, and drug-related causes.
Communicate uncertainty and urgency safely in a consult note.
boardDomains: Foundational immunology and diagnostic reasoning; aligns broadly to the ABIM Rheumatology Blueprint.
units.casePractice: Fictional acute polyarthritis triage vignette: write a one-sentence problem representation and a safety-first differential.
units.assessment: Five-item concept check plus faculty-style self-rubric.

units.title: Musculoskeletal history, examination, synovial fluid, and procedures
objectives: Perform a structured history and joint-focused examination in supervised clinical settings.
Interpret synovial-fluid cell count, crystal microscopy, and culture in clinical context.
State why crystals do not independently exclude infection.
boardDomains: Diagnostic reasoning; procedures and patient safety.
units.casePractice: Fictional hot-knee vignette: order an appropriate diagnostic workup and identify when urgent in-person evaluation is required. No procedure is performed in this course.
units.assessment: Image-free synovial-fluid interpretation worksheet and safety checkpoint.

units.title: Rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory polyarthritis
objectives: Differentiate common inflammatory polyarthritis patterns and important mimics.
Explain treat-to-target reasoning, disease activity assessment, and shared decision-making at a conceptual level.
Recognize medication monitoring and infection-risk questions that need supervised clinical follow-up.
boardDomains: Inflammatory arthritis; therapeutics and longitudinal care.
units.casePractice: Fictional symmetric small-joint inflammatory arthritis: identify discriminating history, exam, laboratory, and imaging information.
units.assessment: Original single-best-answer questions plus a 250-word evidence-to-plan memo.

units.title: Spondyloarthritis, psoriatic disease, and regional pain
objectives: Recognize axial versus peripheral spondyloarthritis patterns and extra-articular clues.
Separate enthesitis, dactylitis, inflammatory back pain, and common mechanical mimics.
Plan referral and multidisciplinary considerations without claiming treatment authority.
units.casePractice: Fictional inflammatory back-pain pattern case: generate a prioritized differential and identify non-rheumatic red flags.
units.assessment: Short-answer pattern-comparison grid.

units.title: Crystal arthritis, osteoarthritis, bone, and metabolic disease
objectives: Compare gout, CPP crystal arthritis, septic arthritis, and osteoarthritis presentations.
Explain why urate-lowering decisions depend on patient context and guideline-supported shared decisions.
Integrate fracture risk, glucocorticoid exposure, and rehabilitation questions into longitudinal care.
boardDomains: Crystal-induced arthritis; bone and metabolic disease; noninflammatory musculoskeletal disorders.
units.casePractice: Fictional recurrent monoarthritis: explain the diagnostic role and limits of serum urate and synovial microscopy.
units.assessment: Evidence table plus one original MCQ.

units.title: Systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid antibodies
objectives: Organize SLE assessment by organ system, activity, damage, differential diagnosis, and safety.
Describe the role of hydroxychloroquine and the goal of minimizing glucocorticoid exposure as guideline principles, with patient-specific decisions left to treating teams.
Distinguish aPL positivity from clinical antiphospholipid syndrome.
topics: Lupus nephritis and neuropsychiatric warning signs
boardDomains: Systemic autoimmune/connective-tissue disease; thrombosis and pregnancy considerations.
units.casePractice: Fictional SLE follow-up: identify organ-threatening features that should trigger urgent supervised evaluation.
units.assessment: Structured organ-system review and two original MCQs.

units.title: Sjögren disease, systemic sclerosis, Raynaud phenomenon, and overlap
objectives: Differentiate primary and secondary Raynaud presentations and identify ischemic red flags.
Link sicca, skin, vascular, pulmonary, renal, and GI features to a systematic connective-tissue disease assessment.
Recognize overlap syndromes and medication/disease mimics.
units.casePractice: Fictional Raynaud-plus-dyspnea case: choose the next safety and organ-screening questions.
units.assessment: Phenotype map and mini-OSCE self-checklist (no patient examination required).

units.title: Vasculitis, autoinflammation, and urgent inflammatory syndromes
objectives: Classify suspected vasculitis by vessel size, organ threat, and competing infection/malignancy/drug explanations.
Interpret ANCA results as supportive data rather than standalone diagnosis.
Escalate visual, renal, pulmonary, neurologic, or ischemic red flags for urgent supervised assessment.
boardDomains: Vasculitides; diagnostic reasoning and urgent disease recognition.
units.casePractice: Fictional pulmonary-renal syndrome: state immediate safety actions and the diagnostic evidence needed before disease-specific therapy.
units.assessment: Original MCQs and a differential-diagnosis matrix.

units.title: Myositis, sarcoid, and rheumatic lung disease
objectives: Differentiate weakness from pain, fatigue, and deconditioning.
Recognize key myositis phenotypes, antibody limitations, malignancy context, and ILD red flags.
Coordinate multidisciplinary reasoning with neurology, pulmonary, dermatology, and oncology.
boardDomains: Inflammatory muscle disease; systemic autoimmune disease and pulmonary manifestations.
units.casePractice: Fictional progressive proximal weakness case: distinguish inflammatory myopathy from endocrine, neurologic, medication, and inherited alternatives.
units.assessment: Interpretation exercise with a malignancy/ILD safety checklist.

units.title: Pediatric-to-adult transition, pregnancy, infection, malignancy, and drug safety
objectives: Identify how age, reproductive plans, infection risk, vaccination, cancer screening, comorbidity, and equity alter rheumatology decision-making.
Use a medication-safety checklist without prescribing or replacing individualized consultation.
Explain limits of extrapolating adult material to pediatric disease.
topics: Malignancy and immune checkpoint inhibitor toxicity
boardDomains: Cross-cutting patient safety, professionalism, systems-based practice.
units.casePractice: Fictional patient planning pregnancy while on an immunomodulator: formulate questions for rheumatology, obstetrics, pharmacy, and primary care.
units.assessment: Team-based referral-and-safety map.

units.title: Imaging, MSK ultrasound, pathology, and rehabilitation
objectives: Match radiograph, ultrasound, MRI, CT, and pathology to a specific clinical question and limitations.
Describe MSK ultrasound as an adjunct that requires training, supervision, and local credentialing.
Integrate physical medicine, orthopedic referral, and function goals.
boardDomains: Diagnostic testing, procedures, musculoskeletal disorders, systems-based care.
units.casePractice: Use linked, licensed-only Open-i examples to create an image-question worksheet; do not copy/rehost images without checking each item’s license.
units.assessment: Modality-to-question matching quiz.

units.title: Evidence, quality improvement, teaching, and capstone consultation
objectives: Critically appraise a guideline and distinguish recommendation strength from individual patient decision-making.
Design a small, de-identified QI or evidence-synthesis project.
Produce a consult-style synthesis that names uncertainty, safety netting, and team roles.
boardDomains: Practice-based learning and improvement; professionalism; systems-based practice.
units.casePractice: Fictional de-identified capstone case: construct a differential, evidence map, and escalation plan; no real patient record is used.
units.assessment: Capstone rubric, self-audit, and oral presentation to peers/mentor.

assignment.title: Fictional de-identified consult synthesis and evidence map
assignment.description: Select one provided fictional case or create a clearly fictional scenario. Produce a 1,000–1,500-word consult-style synthesis: problem representation; prioritized differential; danger/urgency screen; evidence table using at least two primary guideline sources; diagnostic limits; multidisciplinary roles; and a safety-net statement. Do not use real patient data, uploaded records, proprietary question banks, or copied images. This is educational and must be reviewed by a qualified supervisor before any clinical use.

assessment.format: Low-stakes formative quizzes, original question set, evidence appraisals, image-license worksheet, fictional capstone, and self-reflection.
assessment.passingOrCredentialing: No passing score, CME, academic credit, procedure sign-off, board eligibility, certification, licensure, or clinical competency is awarded.
assessment.assessmentAlignment: Questions are original teaching items aligned at high level with ABIM’s publicly available blueprint and ACGME competence themes; they are not ABIM questions or predictive of examination outcome.

studyHours.plan: 100-hour independent-study plan over approximately 18 weeks: 36.439722 observed free specialty-recording hours; 22 hours guideline/readings; 18 hours structured case/evidence exercises; 12 hours question review and retrieval practice; 12 hours fictional capstone/reflection. Planned original clips are not counted because they have not been produced, uploaded, or duration-verified. BIDMC clinical rotations, continuity clinics, consultations, ultrasound, procedures, research, and conferences are expressly excluded from these lecture/study-hour claims.

mapping.name: Rheumatology Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Actual, distinct ACGME-accredited clinical physician fellowship—not a generic directory category. BIDMC publicly describes a two-year fellowship with optional additional research year. The public overview names 2–3 weekly half-day continuity clinics, inpatient consult responsibility, Musculoskeletal Medicine Unit (BIDMC and Boston Children’s), Lupus Center, faculty electives, second-year diagnostic/procedural ultrasound exposure, conferences, and research. BIDMC’s application page says applicants must complete three years of Internal Medicine or Family Medicine residency before starting. These descriptions are not a complete curriculum and do not expose lecture recordings or credit this course.

boardNames: American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) — Rheumatology Certification Examination
medical.boardStatus: ABIM recognizes Rheumatology as an Internal Medicine subspecialty certification. It is a separate ABIM certification examination; completion of this independent course does not confer certification or examination eligibility.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABIM’s current policy requires prior ABIM Internal Medicine certification at application, accredited rheumatology fellowship training, satisfactory competence, a valid unrestricted and unchallenged medical license, and passing the Rheumatology Certification Examination. ABIM specifies 24 total months and 12 full-time clinical months, with procedural competence. The only stated rheumatology/allergy-immunology dual route is a prospectively approved minimum three-year combined program with defined clinical/continuity requirements; this course creates neither single nor dual eligibility. Policies can change—verify directly with ABIM.

officialProgrammes.name: Rheumatology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Actual, distinct ACGME-accredited clinical physician fellowship—not a generic directory category. BIDMC publicly describes a two-year fellowship with optional additional research year. The public overview names 2–3 weekly half-day continuity clinics, inpatient consult responsibility, Musculoskeletal Medicine Unit (BIDMC and Boston Children’s), Lupus Center, faculty electives, second-year diagnostic/procedural ultrasound exposure, conferences, and research. BIDMC’s application page says applicants must complete three years of Internal Medicine or Family Medicine residency before starting. These descriptions are not a complete curriculum and do not expose lecture recordings or credit this course.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: A 58-year-old has an acutely swollen, hot knee, fever, and a history of gout. Polarized microscopy shows monosodium urate crystals. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: Crystals exclude concomitant septic arthritis.
The finding establishes gout and ends the workup.
Crystals support gout but do not by themselves exclude infection; culture and the clinical context remain important.
Serum urate alone is sufficient to decide whether infection is present.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Crystal identification supports crystal arthritis, but it does not independently rule out infection in a hot joint. The educational point is diagnostic safety, not treatment direction for a real patient.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: A patient has symmetric MCP/PIP synovitis, prolonged morning stiffness, and functional limitation. Which next step best reflects guideline-informed rheumatology reasoning?

options.text: Make a treatment choice using a laboratory result alone.
Integrate inflammatory phenotype, disease activity, function, comorbidity, reproductive plans, infection risk, and shared decision-making.
Assume all symmetric hand pain is rheumatoid arthritis.
Avoid reassessing outcomes after a management change.

practiceQuestions.rationale: RA management principles require longitudinal assessment and patient-centered decisions; no single laboratory test or symptom pattern independently settles diagnosis or regimen.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement most accurately reflects the 2023 EULAR SLE update?

options.text: Hydroxychloroquine is generally recommended for patients with SLE unless contraindicated, with individualized attention to flare and retinal-toxicity risk.
Hydroxychloroquine should be stopped routinely in all patients in remission.
All SLE manifestations can be managed without considering organ involvement.
Antiphospholipid antibodies alone establish thrombotic APS.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The EULAR update recommends hydroxychloroquine unless contraindicated and frames dosing/risk decisions individually. This is a guideline-literacy question, not a dosing instruction.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: A patient with known SLE develops new edema, hypertension, rising creatinine, and active urinary sediment. What is the best educational response?

options.text: Treat it as routine fatigue and defer assessment.
Recognize possible organ-threatening renal involvement and arrange urgent supervised clinical evaluation.
Diagnose lupus nephritis from one symptom only and give a fixed regimen.
Ignore blood pressure because it is not rheumatologic.

practiceQuestions.rationale: New renal warning features require timely clinical assessment and multidisciplinary reasoning. The course cannot diagnose or prescribe for a real person.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: A patient has chronic sinus symptoms, pulmonary infiltrates, hematuria, and a positive PR3-ANCA. Which interpretation is safest?

options.text: PR3-ANCA alone proves the diagnosis and makes tissue or infection evaluation unnecessary.
The phenotype raises concern for ANCA-associated vasculitis, but tests must be interpreted with clinical findings and competing causes such as infection considered.
ANCA testing is never useful in vasculitis evaluation.
Only skin symptoms matter in vasculitis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline supports disease-specific clinical reasoning; serology is not a substitute for phenotype, exclusion of mimics, and appropriate supervised evaluation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: A 72-year-old develops new headache, jaw claudication, and transient visual symptoms. Which course principle applies?

options.text: Visual symptoms can wait for a routine elective follow-up.
Potential ischemic visual symptoms are an urgent safety signal requiring immediate supervised evaluation.
Age excludes inflammatory disease.
A normal musculoskeletal examination rules out vasculitis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: This checks recognition of an organ-threatening vasculitis presentation and escalation, not independent treatment administration.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: A patient has progressive proximal weakness, elevated muscle enzymes, dyspnea, and anti-synthetase antibodies. Which additional concern should be actively assessed?

options.text: Interstitial lung disease and the need for pulmonary collaboration.
Only hand osteoarthritis.
No systemic involvement because the primary symptom is weakness.
A steroid dose copied from an internet case report.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Inflammatory myopathy assessment includes pulmonary risk and multidisciplinary evaluation. The answer does not authorize treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the ABIM rheumatology training/certification boundary?

options.text: Watching lectures alone satisfies the accredited fellowship requirement.
ABIM requires prior ABIM Internal Medicine certification, accredited fellowship training, documented competence, an unrestricted unchallenged license, and passing the examination.
A research course substitutes for all clinical training.
Continuity clinic can be replaced by video viewing.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM lists these requirements. This independent course can support knowledge acquisition only; it cannot confer credit, certification, licensure, or eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: A patient has hand pain, bony DIP enlargement, and brief stiffness without synovitis. Which reasoning move is best?

options.text: Assume inflammatory arthritis without considering osteoarthritis or other noninflammatory causes.
Use pattern, examination, function, and appropriate testing to distinguish inflammatory from noninflammatory disease and retain a differential.
Diagnose from an imaging report without clinical correlation.
Treat all hand pain as a procedural indication.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The core skill is pattern-based differential diagnosis with clinical correlation, not a reflex label.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the correct licensing practice when using an authentic image found through NLM Open-i?

options.text: All Open-i images may be copied because Open-i is free to view.
Inspect the individual image’s source and license; link when rights are unclear, and do not rehost without permission.
Remove attribution if an image is used for education.
Assume MedPix contributor material is public domain.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NLM states that Open-i cannot grant permissions and that image-specific licenses/source rights govern reuse.

title: Sexual Medicine Fellowship

prerequisites.intendedLearner: Postgraduate physician-level independent learner, typically with a urology/gynecology/primary-care or other relevant clinical foundation; this independent course is open for education and does not verify credentials.
priorKnowledge: Clinical history-taking, differential diagnosis and evidence appraisal
Basic endocrine/reproductive physiology and medication safety
Professional ethics, privacy, informed consent and scope of practice
prerequisites.entryRequirements: No enrollment prerequisite, selection, credential or institutional eligibility decision is asserted. Hopkins official programme page does not expose a complete current applicant checklist in the fetched public text.

objectives: Integrate sexual concerns with general medical, psychological, medication, relationship and reproductive context.
Take an inclusive, permission-based and trauma-informed sexual history.
Build differential diagnoses and select targeted evaluation using current primary guidance.
Interpret risk, uncertainty and patient-defined goals across erectile, ejaculatory, orgasmic, desire, pain, hormonal, fertility and survivorship presentations.
Explain options, risks, contraindications and referral boundaries without authorizing unsupervised care.
Critically appraise sexual-medicine evidence and communicate limitations.

units.title: Scope, sexual response, and clinical reasoning foundations
objectives: Explain sexual medicine as the interaction between sexual concerns and general health without treating normal variation as disease.
Organize symptoms by desire, arousal, orgasm/ejaculation, pain, function, relationship context, and personally meaningful distress.
Separate evidence, consensus, expert opinion, and unresolved uncertainty.
topics: Medical, medication, relationship, and cultural contributors
Patient-centred goals, shared decision-making, stigma and distress
Clinical reasoning: symptom representation, differential, red flags, follow-up
boardDomains: Underlying specialty knowledge only; no sexual-medicine board blueprint identified.
units.casePractice: Map a fictional referral question to a problem representation and identify what remains unknown.
units.assessment: Concept map plus uncertainty statement; do not diagnose from isolated symptoms.

units.title: Sexual history, consent, communication, and inclusion
objectives: Obtain a permission-based, confidential, nonjudgmental history tailored to the patient.
Distinguish gender identity, sex assigned at birth, sexual orientation, behaviours, partners, and reproductive intentions.
Identify trauma, coercion, safety concerns, and when to pause, offer choice, or refer.
topics: Inclusive language, pronouns, disability, aging and culture
boardDomains: Communication, professionalism, ethics and patient safety in the learner’s entry specialty.
units.casePractice: Recorded or written role-play using a fictional adult; no real patient information.
units.assessment: Structured sexual-history OSCE with consent, open questions, confidentiality and recap.

units.title: Sexual pain, vulvar pain, and pelvic-floor differential
objectives: Classify pain by location, timing, provocation, onset, and duration.
Construct a differential that includes infection, dermatosis, GSM, pelvic-floor, neuropathic and other causes.
Describe consent-first examination choices and referral boundaries.
topics: Dyspareunia, vulvodynia and pain with orgasm
Focused history, external/genital exam when indicated, cotton-swab mapping and tests to exclude specific causes
Pelvic-floor dysfunction, trauma, psychosexual support and multimodal care
boardDomains: Gynecologic/urologic examination reasoning and pain assessment; not procedural competency.
units.casePractice: Read the published dysorgasmia case link; identify data gaps and alternative causes. Do not copy images or patient details into coursework.
units.assessment: Differential and consent-based workup plan scored for red flags, alternatives and follow-up.

units.title: Erectile dysfunction: assessment, risk, and diagnostic strategy
objectives: Take medical, sexual, psychosocial and medication history and select physical/laboratory assessment.
Recognize ED as a marker that may warrant cardiovascular risk assessment rather than a diagnosis by itself.
Interpret selected tests and explain when specialist evaluation is useful.
topics: Erectile physiology; vascular, neurogenic, endocrine, medication, postsurgical and psychosexual factors
Validated symptom measurement; morning testosterone; selective testing
Post-prostate-cancer concerns and limits of penile rehabilitation claims
boardDomains: Urology/sexual function knowledge; maps to guideline-based case reasoning, not a separate board blueprint.
units.casePractice: Use the Johns Hopkins ED webinar as an introductory lecture, then compare its framing with the AUA guideline.
units.assessment: Interpret a fictional ED referral and distinguish risk marker from causal diagnosis.

units.title: Erectile dysfunction: treatment choices, safety, and reconstructive options
objectives: Compare patient-centred treatment options and explain benefits, burdens and contraindications.
Identify nitrate/PDE5 inhibitor safety concerns and the need for appropriate assessment and counseling around invasive treatments.
Discuss device, injection and prosthesis options conceptually without teaching unsupervised procedures.
topics: Lifestyle and comorbidity management; PDE5 inhibitors and nitrate contraindication
Vacuum devices, intraurethral/intracavernosal therapies and priapism precautions
Prosthesis counseling, surgery and expectations; role of mental-health support
boardDomains: Therapeutics, contraindications, informed consent and surgical decision-making; no procedure competence claim.
units.casePractice: Build a shared-decision comparison for fictional medication, device and referral options.
units.assessment: Treatment reasoning matrix; penalty for missing contraindication or implying self-administration training.

units.title: Testosterone, hypogonadism, and sexual function
objectives: Apply the AUA diagnostic framework and avoid diagnosing from nonspecific symptoms or one test.
Differentiate primary from secondary patterns using targeted labs and clinical context.
Explain exogenous testosterone’s potential fertility effects and monitoring/safety considerations.
topics: Two early-morning tests on separate occasions plus symptoms/signs
LH, prolactin, hematocrit and context-directed evaluation
Testosterone therapy, fertility intentions, uncertainty and shared decision-making
boardDomains: Endocrine/urology knowledge relevant to entry specialty; no sexual-medicine board exam.
units.casePractice: Interpret a fictional pair of laboratory results and fertility preference without writing a prescription.
units.assessment: Evidence-based short answer; earns credit for a differential and explicitly stated limits.

units.title: Ejaculatory and orgasmic disorders
objectives: Differentiate lifelong/acquired premature ejaculation, delayed ejaculation, anejaculation and orgasmic pain by history.
Use distress, control, context, comorbid ED, medications and relationship effects rather than timing alone.
Appraise dated consensus recommendations and separate evidence from local regulatory status.
topics: Delayed ejaculation/anorgasmia, medication effects and post-procedure changes
Orgasmic pain and referral triggers; evidence and outcome measurement
boardDomains: Sexual-function differential and therapeutics; no independent board blueprint.
units.casePractice: Compare two fictional complaints and identify why latency or orgasm alone is insufficient for diagnosis.
units.assessment: Differential table with one evidence-age caveat and a patient-centred outcome.

units.title: Desire, arousal, and female sexual function
objectives: Distinguish distressing dysfunction from asexual identity, responsive desire, mismatch, or non-pathological variation.
Use biopsychosocial evaluation for HSDD and assess medication, mood, health and relationship contributors.
Explain that testosterone concentration alone does not diagnose HSDD and discuss off-label treatment evidence cautiously.
topics: Desire/arousal/orgasm/pain domains and contextual sexual response
Decreased Sexual Desire Screener and clinical evaluation
Evidence, safety and limits of androgen treatment; psychotherapy and multimodal care
boardDomains: Gynecologic and general sexual-function reasoning; not exam eligibility.
units.casePractice: Draft a fictional HSDD assessment that explicitly includes distress and patient goals.
units.assessment: Biopsychosocial formulation and evidence-based options with uncertainty.

units.title: GSM, menopause, and pelvic health
objectives: Recognize symptom-based GSM assessment and coexisting genitourinary/pelvic conditions.
Describe shared decision-making across local, systemic, nonhormonal and referral options without a universal stepwise algorithm.
Identify when sexual pain needs infection, dermatosis, pelvic-floor or cancer-risk evaluation.
topics: Local low-dose vaginal estrogen as one option in the guideline, with patient-specific discussion
Pelvic-floor physical therapy and sexual counselling; cancer-related considerations

unitMap.text: Scope, sexual response, and clinical reasoning foundations
coveredTopics: Medical, medication, relationship, and cultural contributors
Patient-centred goals, shared decision-making, stigma and distress
Clinical reasoning: symptom representation, differential, red flags, follow-up

unitMap.text: Sexual history, consent, communication, and inclusion
coveredTopics: Inclusive language, pronouns, disability, aging and culture

unitMap.text: Sexual pain, vulvar pain, and pelvic-floor differential
coveredTopics: Dyspareunia, vulvodynia and pain with orgasm
Focused history, external/genital exam when indicated, cotton-swab mapping and tests to exclude specific causes
Pelvic-floor dysfunction, trauma, psychosexual support and multimodal care

unitMap.text: Erectile dysfunction: assessment, risk, and diagnostic strategy
coveredTopics: Erectile physiology; vascular, neurogenic, endocrine, medication, postsurgical and psychosexual factors
Validated symptom measurement; morning testosterone; selective testing
Post-prostate-cancer concerns and limits of penile rehabilitation claims

unitMap.text: Erectile dysfunction: treatment choices, safety, and reconstructive options
coveredTopics: Lifestyle and comorbidity management; PDE5 inhibitors and nitrate contraindication
Vacuum devices, intraurethral/intracavernosal therapies and priapism precautions
Prosthesis counseling, surgery and expectations; role of mental-health support

unitMap.text: Testosterone, hypogonadism, and sexual function
coveredTopics: Two early-morning tests on separate occasions plus symptoms/signs
LH, prolactin, hematocrit and context-directed evaluation
Testosterone therapy, fertility intentions, uncertainty and shared decision-making

unitMap.text: Ejaculatory and orgasmic disorders
coveredTopics: Delayed ejaculation/anorgasmia, medication effects and post-procedure changes
Orgasmic pain and referral triggers; evidence and outcome measurement

unitMap.text: Desire, arousal, and female sexual function
coveredTopics: Desire/arousal/orgasm/pain domains and contextual sexual response
Decreased Sexual Desire Screener and clinical evaluation
Evidence, safety and limits of androgen treatment; psychotherapy and multimodal care

unitMap.text: GSM, menopause, and pelvic health
coveredTopics: Local low-dose vaginal estrogen as one option in the guideline, with patient-specific discussion
Pelvic-floor physical therapy and sexual counselling; cancer-related considerations

unitMap.text: STI, reproductive, gender-affirming, and sexual-health interfaces
coveredTopics: CDC 5 Ps, specimen-site reasoning and STI guidance
Identity, behavior, partner structure and gender-affirming multidisciplinary care
Reproductive goals, sexual effects of treatments and referral pathways

unitMap.text: Cancer, treatment effects, survivorship, and sexual function
coveredTopics: Prostate, pelvic and other cancer treatment effects
Pre-treatment fertility preservation and survivorship discussion
Psychosexual counseling, GSM, ED, pain and uncertainty about treatment effects

unitMap.text: Peyronie disease, penile/genitourinary reconstruction, infertility, and scholarly practice
coveredTopics: Penile curvature and stable versus active disease; guideline options and limits
Reconstructive/prosthetic urology and referral to trained teams
Infertility and fertility preservation; clinical/basic research design and outcome measurement

boardNames: No separate U.S. sexual-medicine ABMS specialty/subspecialty board identified; the American Board of Urology is relevant only to underlying urology certification, not this fellowship.
medical.boardStatus: Johns Hopkins’ specific listing states “Non-Standard”; its profile says the programme met Johns Hopkins School of Medicine Graduate Medical Education Committee requirements for equivalency and is certified by SMSNA. Do not label it ACGME-accredited. The ABMS directory checked 2026-10-07 lists no Sexual Medicine physician specialty/subspecialty certificate. No separate U.S. sexual-medicine board examination was identified in the authoritative sources reviewed; underlying primary specialty board routes (for example urology) are separate. The ABU examination information page was not accessible in this review, so no broader claim about every non-ABMS examination is made.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent self-study course does not confer eligibility for any board exam, fellowship, credential, license, or certification. Eligibility for the real Johns Hopkins fellowship is determined by that institution; public materials indicate a post-urology-residency clinical track, but the current individual programme page fetched did not expose complete applicant requirements.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / The Johns Hopkins Hospital
officialProgrammes.name: Sexual Medicine Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official listing states 2 years, accrediting body “Non-Standard,” and GMEC approval of equivalency requirements; it states SMSNA certification. No public didactic-hour or case-volume totals were found.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins Medicine, Brady Urological Institute
officialProgrammes.name: Sexual Medicine and Reconstructive Urology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official detailed programme page describes basic training (12 months), advanced training (12 months), continuous office/OR exposure and ongoing basic-science or clinical research. It does not publish case counts or a lecture-hour ledger. This is the detailed name for the same Johns Hopkins programme, not a second fellowship.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The item packet’s “Sexual Medicine Fellowship” label and Hopkins Brady page’s exact “Sexual Medicine and Reconstructive Urology Fellowship” title are retained as two official labels for one clinical physician programme. Johns Hopkins’ program-specific “Non-Standard” listing and its GMEC equivalency statement are distinguished from generic directory-category language such as “ACGME Accredited or Equivalent.” This course excludes research-only positions as separate physician tracks and does not infer a separate sexual-medicine board or exam. The public programme description shows two 12-month phases and research activity but no complete didactic syllabus, clinical case logs, exact applicant criteria or didactic-hour totals.
sourceCaveats: The Johns Hopkins official programme pages were text-accessible. The specific listing says “Non-Standard”; its GMEC equivalency statement is not ACGME accreditation. The source pages do not disclose exact didactic hours, full rotation schedule, case minimums, or a complete applicant checklist.

The ABMS certificate directory was checked 2026-10-07; it contains no separate Sexual Medicine certificate. This supports only the narrow ABMS finding. No separate U.S. sexual-medicine examination was found in the sources reviewed; the ABU information page returned 403, so no assertion is made about every non-ABMS assessment.

AUA ED guidance was published 2018; AUA Peyronie guidance is based on evidence through 2015; ACOG persistent vulvar pain guidance is 2016. Consult current amended guidance and local regulatory labeling before clinical use.

The AUA testosterone, male infertility and GSM pages are official public guidance; verify their amendment/update state at point of use. Clinical recommendations are contextual, not patient-specific directions.

ISSM/ISSWSH HSDD full text is open-access; a testosterone level alone does not diagnose HSDD. The PE source is the 2014 ISSM guideline update and may be outdated; it is used only to teach its published definition with an explicit date caveat.

CDC page labels the 2021 STI guideline current, with last review listed June 13, 2023; product availability/other updates may change. CDC sexual-history guide was updated/reviewed June 26, 2024. WPATH SOC8 dates from 2022.
ASCO guideline citation is freely readable at PubMed as an abstract; full article may require authorized access.
Public view is not a license to copy/rehost. Clinical case links are for individual reading only. No patient images or records are copied.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with erectile dysfunction reports use of a long-acting organic nitrate for angina. Which counseling statement is the safest guideline-aligned next step?

options.text: Prescribe a PDE5 inhibitor at a low dose and schedule follow-up.
Do not prescribe a PDE5 inhibitor while the patient is using organic nitrates; reassess the treatment plan and risks.
Use two PDE5 inhibitors together to overcome the nitrate effect.
Switch immediately to intracavernosal injection without counseling.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AUA ED guidance excludes PDE5 inhibitors for patients using organic nitrates. A careful medication review and shared decision-making are required; this scenario does not authorize a particular alternative treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A man reports fatigue and low libido. His total testosterone is 278 ng/dL from one afternoon draw during an acute illness. Which interpretation best follows AUA guidance?

options.text: This single value establishes testosterone deficiency and treatment should begin.
The result alone is insufficient; evaluate symptoms/signs and obtain two separate early-morning measurements when clinically appropriate.
A questionnaire score alone establishes the diagnosis.
No further assessment is needed because fatigue is specific to low testosterone.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AUA guidance requires compatible symptoms/signs and two early-morning total testosterone tests on separate occasions; acute illness and nonspecific symptoms can confound interpretation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with azoospermia and future fertility goals asks for exogenous testosterone to address low libido. What is the key counseling point in the AUA/ASRM male-infertility guideline?

options.text: Exogenous testosterone is first-line because it improves sperm production.
Do not prescribe exogenous testosterone to a male interested in current or future fertility; complete reproductive evaluation and discuss appropriate referral.
Fertility is unaffected by exogenous testosterone.
A semen analysis is unnecessary if serum testosterone is low.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline says clinicians should not prescribe exogenous testosterone to men interested in current or future fertility. Evaluation and individualized options depend on the cause; this course does not prescribe treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A postmenopausal patient reports low desire but no personal distress; her partner is concerned about the frequency of sex. Which is the best initial interpretation?

options.text: Diagnose HSDD based solely on partner distress.
A serum testosterone result is sufficient to diagnose HSDD.
Clarify the patient’s own goals and distress and assess context; a desire difference alone does not establish a disorder.
Recommend testosterone before taking a sexual history.

practiceQuestions.rationale: HSDD evaluation is biopsychosocial and requires distress in the patient; serum testosterone is not a diagnostic test for HSDD. Shared decision-making starts with the patient’s goals.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has localized provoked vulvar pain for four months. What should be done before assigning idiopathic vulvodynia?

options.text: Assume pain is psychogenic if visual inspection is normal.
Evaluate for specific treatable causes, take a detailed history and consider a consent-based examination including pain mapping.
Order HPV testing as the sole diagnostic test.
Proceed directly to surgery.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACOG describes vulvodynia as a diagnosis of exclusion and recommends history, examination, evaluation for infection when indicated, and cotton-swab localization; care is individualized and often multidisciplinary.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with Peyronie disease requests reconstructive surgery. Which factor is central to AUA guideline surgical candidacy assessment?

options.text: Surgery is best during rapidly changing curvature.
Assess whether disease is stable and document deformity, erectile function, distress and patient goals.
A patient-reported estimate alone is sufficient.
Penile curvature always predicts ED refractory to medication.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AUA guideline recommends assessing surgical candidates for stable disease and documenting objective deformity, erectile function, functional impact and distress to support informed decisions. Guideline age is a caveat; check for updates.

practiceQuestions.stem: During an oncology follow-up, the patient has not raised sexual function concerns. Which approach is supported by the ASCO guideline abstract?

options.text: Wait until the patient independently raises sex.
A member of the care team should initiate a discussion of sexual health and treatment-related dysfunction and offer appropriate psychosocial/psychosexual support.
Discuss only erectile function with male patients.
Assume sexual dysfunction is irreversible after cancer therapy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline recommends that a member of the team initiate sexual-health discussion and offer psychosocial or psychosexual counseling. PubMed provides the abstract; full article access may require subscription.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinician needs to determine which STI specimens are appropriate. The patient describes sexual practices that differ from the clinician’s assumptions based on gender identity. What is the best next step?

options.text: Use identity labels to infer the practices and sites involved.
Ask permission and use open-ended, behavior- and anatomy-specific questions; tailor testing to the history and current guidance.
Avoid the sexual history unless symptoms are present.
Ask only about marital status.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC advises a tailored, non-assumptive history and describes practices/sites as relevant to testing. Gender identity does not determine a person’s partners or practices.
practiceQuestions.domain: Sexual history, STI prevention and communication

practiceQuestions.stem: A published case report describes pain immediately after orgasm that later resolved. How should a learner use this resource?

options.text: Copy the patient’s case details and any image into a teaching file.
Treat one case report as proof that the same cause explains future cases.
Link to the report, appraise its limitations, build an original fictional discussion case, and do not copy images or patient records.
Use it to authorize unsupervised examination or treatment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The linked publication is an authentic, de-identified case report, but a single case cannot establish general causation. No image or patient record is copied; free access is not blanket reuse permission.
practiceQuestions.domain: Evidence appraisal, privacy and ethical case-based learning

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient’s self-estimated intravaginal ejaculatory latency is about one minute. Which additional feature is essential to the older ISSM consensus definition of lifelong premature ejaculation?

options.text: Latency alone is sufficient.
Inability to delay ejaculation and negative personal consequences such as distress or bother are also part of the definition.
A PDE5 inhibitor response confirms the diagnosis.
A physical examination is never useful.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2014 ISSM update describes lifelong PE using latency, inability to delay, and negative personal consequences; it is an older consensus source and requires current guideline review.

title: Transitional Year Residency
level: Clinical physician residency — cross-disciplinary PGY-1 category-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Appropriate medical foundational knowledge; the material is aimed at postgraduate-level learners and is not lay emergency instruction.
For real clinical activity: active enrolment in an appropriate programme, local credentialing, named supervision, and site policies are required; this course supplies none.
Use only fictitious/de-identified practice material. Do not enter, upload, or discuss identifiable patient information.
Current local emergency, infection-control, medication, and escalation policies override this curriculum.
A current source-check habit: archived recordings support concepts but do not establish current treatment, dose, or institutional policy.
objectives: Describe the actual scope and accreditation boundary of a Transitional Year and distinguish it from specialty-board certification.
Apply structured clinical reasoning, uncertainty management, supervision, and escalation concepts to fictional/de-identified scenarios.
Use current primary sources for infection prevention, emergency response, prevention, stewardship, and handoffs.
Demonstrate a structured I-PASS handoff with receiver synthesis in a simulation.
Recognize the limits of independent study for procedures, acute care, pediatrics, surgery, and clinical judgement.
Plan a privacy-safe QI/reflective portfolio and identify the need for local governance.

Describe why sepsis assessment includes alternative diagnoses and repeated reassessment.
State the stewardship roles of culture interpretation, review, de-escalation discussion, and communication with the team.
units.casePractice: Review the linked CC-BY rickettsial-sepsis case as a differential/diagnostic-safety exercise. Link only; do not rehost figures or generalize a rare case into treatment advice.
units.assessment: Infection-prevention and stewardship concept map; includes a reassessment and escalation step.

units.title: Neurologic change, delirium, geriatrics, and serious illness communication
objectives: Separate acute cognitive change, focal neurologic concern, and chronic functional vulnerability in a fictional scenario.
Recognize a negative test can require reassessment when clinical concern persists.
Frame goals-of-care communication as supervised, patient-centered work rather than a scripted decision.
topics: serious illness and goals of care
units.casePractice: Use an external licensed case only to analyze diagnostic uncertainty; for communication practice use a fictional case and a trained facilitator.
units.assessment: Reflective response: uncertainty, escalation, and one patient-preference question.

units.title: Emergency, surgery, pediatrics, and first-contact assessment
objectives: Describe the limits of an independent module for emergency, surgical, and pediatric care.
Use an initial-assessment framework to recognize time-sensitive illness or injury and activate local help.
Identify the need for age-appropriate, specialty-specific supervision and local policy.
units.casePractice: Discuss the linked CC-BY pediatric appendicitis case as a diagnostic-reassessment exercise. No surgical, airway, or pediatric procedure is simulated or authorized.
units.assessment: Paper triage/escalation exercise, assessed for recognition of scope limits and communication.

units.title: Ambulatory medicine, prevention, addiction, and transitions of care
objectives: Use the current schedule and recommendation sources to locate, not memorize, preventive-care guidance.
Prepare a safe post-hospitalization handoff that states ownership, follow-up, and return precautions.
Recognize substance-use care and social needs as longitudinal, interprofessional work.
units.casePractice: Build a fictional discharge-to-clinic plan; verify a single current prevention question using the source rather than the lecture.
units.assessment: Structured I-PASS handoff and prevention-source navigation task.

units.title: Equity, trauma-informed care, ethics, and patient advocacy
objectives: Use trauma-informed and respectful communication in a fictional encounter without stereotyping.
Identify an ethical uncertainty and the appropriate supervisory, ethics, or social-work resource.
Explain how social context and access can alter a safe plan without making unsupported assumptions.
units.casePractice: Write a strengths-based, fictional case reflection that identifies interpreter/social-work/ethics resources and avoids exposing patient information.
units.assessment: Facilitator-scored communication reflection; no role-play with real patients.

units.title: Teamwork, handoffs, feedback, EHR documentation, and quality improvement
objectives: Deliver the five elements of I-PASS and close the loop through synthesis by receiver.
Describe the safety role of clear documentation, feedback, and escalation without copying an institutional note template.
Develop a narrow QI question with a process measure, balancing measure, and privacy safeguard.
units.casePractice: Use a fictional patient summary for a simulated handoff. Do not paste, upload, or retain real clinical documentation.
units.assessment: I-PASS observed structured exercise plus a one-page de-identified/synthetic QI charter.

units.title: Elective alignment, scholarship, career planning, and reflective synthesis
objectives: Compare a future specialty’s written PGY-1 prerequisites with a TY programme’s published rotations.
Use elective planning to identify learning needs without claiming that a self-study course establishes eligibility.
Produce a reflective portfolio that documents sources, limitations, feedback, and next supervised learning steps.
units.casePractice: Compare one intended advanced specialty’s current ACGME prerequisite text with the CHA sample schedule; record any mismatch as a question for the programme director/board.
units.assessment: Portfolio review with a limitation statement and a source-currency log.

assignment.title: Transitional-Year Foundations Portfolio
components: A source-currency log for six clinical questions (authority, date, limitation).
Two original fictional problem representations with differential, uncertainty, contingency, and escalation language.
One simulated I-PASS handoff with a receiver-synthesis transcript.
One privacy-safe, synthetic QI charter: aim, process measure, balancing measure, supervisor/governance questions.
One rotation/elective alignment memo comparing a future speciality prerequisite with published TY requirements.
assignment.submissionBoundary: No patient records, screenshots, EHR extracts, real images, local protocols, or protected assessment materials. A portfolio is educational work only and cannot be submitted as residency credit.

mapping.name: Transitional Year Residency
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: CHA’s directory marks Transitional Year ACGME accredited. CHA describes a one-year programme intertwined with Internal Medicine. Its public curriculum labels its 52-week block chart a sample: inpatient medicine 10–12 weeks, critical care 4–6, general surgery 4, emergency medicine 4, pediatrics 2–4, ambulatory medicine 4, night medicine/night ICU 8–10, elective 8, and vacation 4. It publicly describes Tuesday four-hour protected core inpatient teaching, and its surgery description states direct supervision. These are public programme descriptions, not a guarantee of an individual schedule, case volume, employment, or access.

officialProgrammes.name: Transitional Year Residency
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: CHA’s directory marks Transitional Year ACGME accredited. CHA describes a one-year programme intertwined with Internal Medicine. Its public curriculum labels its 52-week block chart a sample: inpatient medicine 10–12 weeks, critical care 4–6, general surgery 4, emergency medicine 4, pediatrics 2–4, ambulatory medicine 4, night medicine/night ICU 8–10, elective 8, and vacation 4. It publicly describes Tuesday four-hour protected core inpatient teaching, and its surgery description states direct supervision. These are public programme descriptions, not a guarantee of an individual schedule, case volume, employment, or access.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This entry covers the one declared programme (Cambridge Health Alliance). It transparently studies broad PGY-1 foundations relevant to its public rotations. It does not merge the unrelated nuclear-medicine/radiology material in the supplied user outline, invent an Emory/Harvard nuclear programme, or assert volumes, equipment, dual-board eligibility, or proprietary didactics.
sourceCaveats: Institutional pages describe public curriculum and sample schedules; they do not prove an individual resident’s rotations, competency, volume, or outcomes.
ACGME programme requirements and Milestones are accreditation/assessment frameworks. They are not an independent board blueprint, and this entry makes no certification claim.
UCSF Grand Rounds recordings are relevant foundations but not CHA materials, not a TY lecture set, not a substitute for current guidelines, and may be dated even when accessible.
The exact selected durations are playlist metadata observations, not estimates. YouTube rate-limited later per-video metadata requests, so publication dates are null rather than guessed.
Linked case reports are authentic published and consented/licensed resources, but individual cases are not generalizable clinical protocols. They are linked, not rehosted.
The supplied user outline is predominantly nuclear-medicine/radiology material and contains unsupported or out-of-scope assertions. It was not imported into this Transitional Year entry.
